case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old Caucasian woman presented with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, and pruritus. She had been admitted twice previously to an outside hospital where a bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and a biopsy of an incidental 1.6 cm right lower‑lobe lung nodule were performed without a definitive diagnosis. Her past medical history was notable for rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate for 8 years and infliximab for 6 years; methotrexate and infliximab were discontinued after elevated liver enzymes were noted, and she was started on prednisone 40 mg daily.

On arrival she was febrile to 103 °F, tachycardic, and had painless jaundice. She denied sick contacts, consumption of unpasteurized milk, or undercooked meat. She reported that her fever began two days after a road trip from Michigan to Florida, during which she spent six days in Pittsburg, Kansas, where she rode horses.

Physical examination showed an alert, oriented patient with icteric sclerae; respiratory rate was 18/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and no hepatosplenomegaly or abdominal tenderness. The remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed: hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, WBC 7.9 ×10⁹/L (40% neutrophils, 43% lymphocytes, 7% monocytes), platelets 230 ×10⁹/L; ALT 252 IU/L, AST 173 IU/L, ALP 375 IU/L, total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL, albumin 2.5 g/dL. Autoimmune markers were negative except for rheumatoid factor and anti‑CCP. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Chest X‑ray showed a right lower‑lobe pulmonary nodule; chest CT confirmed a 1.3 cm nodule in the same location. Abdominal CT demonstrated normal liver, pancreas, spleen, and adrenals.

Review of outside records indicated bronchial washings grew only Candida albicans; cytology showed mixed inflammatory cells without organisms on GMS stain. CT‑guided needle biopsy of the lung nodule showed acute and chronic inflammation with scattered yeast elements consistent with Candida, but no granulomas or tumor. CMV PCR and hepatitis serologies were negative; EBV PCR was positive (1959 copies/cc) with IgG VCA positive, IgM VCA negative. RPR and QuantiFERON‑TB tests were negative; serum cryptococcal antigen was negative.

Empiric vancomycin and piperacillin‑tazobactam were discontinued after cultures remained sterile. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal function without vegetations. On hospital day 2, an ultrasound‑guided liver biopsy demonstrated granulomatous hepatitis; acid‑fast stain was negative. Steroids were restarted. Serologies for Brucella, Bartonella, and Q fever were negative. Liver biopsy immunohistochemistry and in‑situ hybridization were negative for EBV.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Candida colonization considered but deemed non‑pathogenic because cultures grew only Candida albicans and lung biopsy showed only scattered yeast without granulomas. | "Bronchial washings had grown only Candida albicans... biopsy... scattered yeast elements consistent with candida species, with no evidence of granulomas or tumor."
2. Cytomegalovirus infection excluded by negative PCR. | "CMV PCR ... were negative."
3. Acute viral hepatitis excluded by negative hepatitis serologies. | "CMV PCR and hepatitis serologies were negative."
4. Epstein‑Barr virus infection deemed unlikely; low‑level PCR positivity without IgM, and liver biopsy negative for EBV by in‑situ hybridization. | "EBV blood PCR came back positive... IgM VCA negative... liver biopsy immunohistochemical stain with in situ hybridization studies was also negative for EBV."
5. Tuberculosis ruled out by negative QuantiFERON‑TB test and absence of acid‑fast organisms on biopsy. | "Serum RPR and QuantiFERON test for tuberculosis were negative. ... acid fast stain, and subsequently steroids were restarted."
6. Cryptococcosis excluded by negative serum cryptococcal antigen. | "Serum cryptococcal antigen from outside hospital was negative."
7. Brucellosis, Bartonellosis, and Q fever excluded by negative serologies. | "Cryptococcal antigen and Brucella, Bartonella and Q fever serologies were all negative."
8. Drug‑induced liver injury considered (methotrexate, infliximab) but discontinued prior to admission; liver biopsy showed granulomatous rather than toxic injury pattern. | "She had elevated liver enzymes with subsequent discontinuation of methotrexate and infliximab."
9. Autoimmune hepatitis considered but antimitochondrial antibodies and other autoimmune markers were negative. | "Autoimmune markers, including serum antimitochondrial antibodies, were negative."
10. Bacterial sepsis ruled out by persistently negative blood and urine cultures despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Blood cultures and urine culture remained negative."
11. Histoplasmosis favored after travel to endemic area (Kansas), immunosuppression (TNF‑α inhibitor), granulomatous hepatitis on biopsy, and later identified narrow‑based budding yeast on GMS stain. | "Patient endorsed horseback riding in Pittsburg... liver biopsy consistent with granulomatous hepatitis... fungal organism ... suggestive of histoplasmosis."

case_prompt:
A 16‑year‑old girl presented to the otolaryngology clinic with painless swelling of the neck and later to the physical medicine and rehabilitation clinic for hip and low‑back pain that resembled spondyloarthropathy. Prior treatment with nonspecific antibiotics had not reduced the size of the cervical lymph nodes. She denied cough, night sweats, or weight loss for the preceding two months. Family history was notable for her father’s treatment for tuberculosis ten years earlier. She lived in a crowded, low‑socioeconomic household and had no known underlying disease.

On examination she was pale, temperature 37.8 °C, blood pressure 120/80 mm Hg, weight 45 kg (3‑10th percentile). Heart and lung sounds were normal, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. A 2 × 2 cm solid, painless right cervical lymph node was palpable. Hip examination revealed tenderness, limited range of motion, and a gait disturbance.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, white blood cell count 5,800/mm³, platelets 704 × 10³/mm³, C‑reactive protein 104 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 74 mm/h, uric acid 5.2 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase 192 U/L. Brucella agglutination test was negative; peripheral smear was unremarkable.

Cervical ultrasonography demonstrated hypoechoic lymphadenopathy. Chest radiograph revealed hilar lymphadenopathy. Thoracic computed tomography identified a Ghon complex in the right lung and findings suspicious for a Pott’s abscess. Thoracic magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a Pott’s abscess involving the T8, T9, and T10 vertebrae. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showed medullary trabecular edema of the right femoral head and neck together with lobular cystic lesions in the peripheral muscle groups.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent cervical lymphadenopathy despite antibiotics suggests a non‑pyogenic cause such as mycobacterial infection rather than typical bacterial lymphadenitis. | "She had been treated with nonspecific antibiotics for cervical lymph nodes, but the size of the lymph nodes did not change with this treatment."
2. Brucellosis was considered because of musculoskeletal involvement, but the serologic test was negative, making it unlikely. | "The Brucella agglutination test was negative."
3. Spondyloarthropathy was a clinical consideration given hip and low‑back pain, yet imaging showed vertebral destruction and an abscess rather than the sacroiliac changes typical of spondyloarthropathy. | "Thoracic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a Pott's abscess involving the T8, T9, and T10 vertebrae."
4. Pyogenic septic arthritis/osteomyelitis could explain joint pain, but the lack of acute systemic signs, normal uric acid, and the presence of a Ghon complex favor a chronic granulomatous process. | "Thoracic computed tomography (CT) revealed a Ghon complex in the right lung and was suspicious for a Pott's abscess."
5. Tuberculosis was supported by a history of household exposure, characteristic imaging (Ghon complex, Pott’s abscess, medullary edema of the femoral head), and elevated inflammatory markers, leading to the final diagnosis. | "Thoracic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed a Pott's abscess involving the T8, T9, and T10 vertebrae."

case_prompt:
A 53‑year‑old woman presented to the physical medicine, rehabilitation and rheumatology department with right‑sided inguinal, hip and knee pain radiating from the right groin to the knee. The pain had begun one week prior, was constant, worsened with rest, and was accompanied by a prior episode of right ankle pain and slight swelling 10 days earlier that lasted three days. She also reported a long‑standing intermittent backache and a six‑month history of abdominal pain. An abdominal ultrasound performed during follow‑up by general surgery revealed a solid hepatic mass. 

Physical examination showed loss of lumbar lordosis, restricted waist movement due to pain, a positive right sacroiliac compression test, a positive FABERE test on the right, warmth and tenderness of the right knee, and local tenderness in the right upper quadrant. No skin rash or other systemic findings were noted. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the sacroiliac joints demonstrated right iliac focal bone‑marrow edema adjacent to the sacroiliac junction and two cystic lesions at the iliac front adjacent to the right hip joint. Abdominal computed tomography identified a well‑defined 55 × 48 mm hypodense lesion with a superior calcification described as a “lily symptom” in hepatic segment 3. 

Laboratory investigations performed for sacroiliitis and arthritis etiology revealed: RF negative, anti‑CCP negative, anti‑cardiolipin negative, dsDNA negative, ANA negative, c‑ANCA and p‑ANCA negative, ESR 38 mm/h, CRP 23 mg/L, WBC 7.31 ×10⁹/L, platelets 364 ×10⁹/L. Brucella Wright and Coombs agglutination tests were negative. EBV VCA IgM, EBV VCA IgG and anti‑CMV IgG were positive; EBV EA and anti‑CMV IgM were negative. Knee joint aspiration yielded 60 mL of yellow clear fluid; analysis showed 8,000 leukocytes (30 % mononuclear, 70 % polymorphonuclear) with no organisms on microscopy, negative TB DNA, negative TB real‑time PCR, and no growth on culture. Blood cultures were sterile. Anti‑HBsAg, anti‑HCV and anti‑HIV tests were negative. Echocardiography showed no evidence of infective endocarditis. A PPD test measured 5 mm; sputum smear and culture were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. HLA‑B27 testing was negative.

1. Spondyloarthropathy considered because of sacroiliac involvement and peripheral arthritis, but excluded by negative HLA‑B27, absence of psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, and lack of family history; “HLA‑B27 genetic assay was negative for spondyloarthropathy.” 
2. Brucellosis considered due to peripheral arthritis, but serology was negative; “Brucella Wright and Coombs agglutination tests were negative.” 
3. Tuberculosis considered given joint involvement and endemic exposure, but multiple tests were negative; “Tbc DNA, tbc real time PCR, mycobacterial culture were detected as negative,” “PPD test was 5 mm and sputum culture … showed no Tbc Bacillus.” 
4. Viral arthritides (EBV, CMV) evaluated; serology showed past EBV infection and prior CMV exposure but no acute infection; “EBV VCA Ig M … detected as positive; EBV EA, Anti‑CMV IG m were detected as negative.” 
5. Autoimmune rheumatoid arthritis and other connective‑tissue diseases excluded by negative RF, anti‑CCP, ANA, dsDNA, ANCA; “RF was negative, anti‑CCP was negative, … ANA was negative, c‑ANCA and p‑ANCA were negative.” 
6. Behçet’s disease, sarcoidosis, familial Mediterranean fever, and malignancy considered but ruled out by lack of clinical criteria, normal tumor markers, and imaging; “no history of other diseases which can cause sacroiliitis and peripheral arthritis like SPA … Behcet's disease, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and malignancy.” 
7. Echinococcosis supported by characteristic hepatic lesion with calcified “lily” sign on CT and a high hydatid serology titer; “Hydatid cyst hemagglutination titer test was 1/320 and the patient was diagnosed as hydatid cyst disease.” 
8. Reactive arthritis secondary to the identified echinococcal infestation concluded after exclusion of other causes; “patient is diagnosed as reactive arthritis secondary to echinococcal infestation after all tests.”

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 11‑year‑old girl presented with an 8‑day history of fever (peaking at 39.4 °C every 12 hours), night sweats, subjective weight loss, headaches, dizziness, nausea, intermittent right‑sided abdominal pain, and anorexia. She noted an intermittently pruritic rash on her arms. She denied respiratory symptoms, emesis, or diarrhea.

Past medical history included multiple bronchiolitis hospitalizations before age 2, severe varicella requiring nasogastric feeding at age 4, and hepatitis A at age 7. She was born in Central America, immigrated to the United States 4 years ago, and had consumed unpasteurized cow milk while in Central America. A maternal uncle was diagnosed with tuberculosis >4 years earlier; no recent contact.

On examination the girl was thin (weight 33.1 kg, BMI 15.5 kg/m²). She had enlarged, mobile, nontender cervical lymph nodes bilaterally; no axillary or inguinal nodes. Small erythematous papules were noted on the left antecubital fossa and right first MCP joint. Mild right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness was present without hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory studies on day of illness (DOI) 9 showed leukopenia, anemia, mildly elevated C‑reactive protein, erythrocyte sedimentation rate >145 mm/hr, and elevated AST/ALT. Cerebrospinal fluid was acellular with normal protein and glucose. Fourth‑generation HIV‑1 antigen‑antibody test was positive; HIV‑1 RNA PCR revealed 294,000 copies/mL in plasma and 504 copies/mL in CSF; CD4 count was 52 cells/mm³.

Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated innumerable small pulmonary nodules and extensive lymphadenopathy involving cervical, axillary, hilar, mediastinal, and retroperitoneal regions; the largest retroperitoneal node measured 4.4 cm.

Bone‑marrow biopsy showed hypocellularity with non‑caseating granulomas. Cervical lymph‑node biopsy revealed plasmacytosis and increased histiocytes without malignancy. Acid‑fast bacillus, Fite, and methenamine silver stains were negative in both specimens. Bronchoscopy noted no airway edema, erythema, or secretions. Evaluation for tuberculosis and non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection was negative, including QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, mycobacterial cultures, and TB PCR from sputum, BAL fluid, lymph‑node tissue, blood, stool, and CSF. Serum antibodies to *Toxoplasma gondii*, *Treponema pallidum*, *Brucella* spp., *Coccidioides immitis*, and *Histoplasma capsulatum* were negative.

Tuberculosis considered due to fever, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary nodules; excluded by negative QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, negative mycobacterial cultures, negative TB PCR from multiple sites, and lack of granulomatous necrosis on pathology. | "Evaluation for tuberculosis (TB) and non‑TB mycobacterial infections was negative, including QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, mycobacterial cultures, and/or TB PCR..."

3. Coccidioidomycosis considered as another endemic fungal infection; excluded by negative serum antibodies to *Coccidioides immitis*. | "Serum antibodies to ... Coccidioides immitis ... were negative."
4. Cryptococcosis considered in advanced HIV; excluded by negative serum antigen testing (implied by lack of mention) and negative methenamine silver stains. | "Acid‑fast bacillus, Fite, and methenamine silver stains were negative in both tissues."
5. Other opportunistic infections (e.g., *Toxoplasma gondii*, *Treponema pallidum*, *Brucella* spp.) considered; excluded by negative serologies. | "Serum antibodies to Toxoplasma gondii, Treponema pallidum, Brucella species ... were negative."

case_prompt: A 60‑year‑old man from a rural area presented to the outpatient clinic with fever, night sweats, headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and migratory pain involving the right hip, right knee, lower back, and back. He reported a history of brucellosis diagnosed two months earlier and a 3‑year history of sheep herding. He also had a 58‑year‑old history of poliomyelitis with right lower‑extremity muscle atrophy. On admission, neurological examination showed a right‑ward deviation of the mouth angle and a shallow left nasolabial fold. Muscle strength was 4/5 in the left upper limb, 2/5 in the left lower limb, 5/5 in the right upper limb, and 4/5 in the right lower limb. Vital signs were temperature 37.5 °C and blood pressure 125/78 mmHg; Glasgow coma score was 15 (E4V5M6). Computed tomography demonstrated an intracerebral hemorrhage in the right basal ganglia that had ruptured into the bilateral lateral ventricles, and magnetic resonance angiography confirmed these findings. Cervical‑vessel ultrasonography revealed bilateral carotid medial thickening with plaque formation. Laboratory studies showed a positive Rose Bengal test and Wright agglutination titer of 1/100 for Brucella, an elevated procalcitonin of 0.219 ng/mL (reference 0–0.046), interleukin‑6 of 66.26 pg/mL (reference 0–7), low high‑density lipoprotein of 0.75 mmol/L (reference 1.03–1.55), D‑dimer 7.25 µg/mL (reference 0–0.50), and fibrinogen degradation products 24.74 µg/mL (reference 0–5).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Imaging confirmed acute intracerebral bleeding, establishing hemorrhage as the principal diagnosis | "CT ... revealed that an intracerebral hemorrhage in the right basal ganglia had broken into bilateral lateral ventricles."
2. MRA excluded vascular malformations or aneurysms that could mimic hemorrhage | "MRA (Figure 1b) revealed that an intracerebral hemorrhage in the right basal ganglia had broken into bilateral lateral ventricles."
3. Elevated D‑dimer and FDP indicated disseminated intravascular coagulation contributing to bleeding risk, supporting a hemorrhagic etiology rather than ischemic stroke | "D‑dimer had increased to 7.25 µg/mL ... and fibrinogen degradation products (FDP) had increased to 24.74 µg/mL."

2. Best breakpoint: Include all presenting data up to the removal of the central venous catheter and its tip culture (negative), i.e., before the cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, endomyocardial biopsy, and coronary angiography that reveal myocarditis. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors differentiate myocarditis from septic shock (negative cultures), from ischemic injury (normal coronary angiography), and consider a post‑COVID‑19 immune mechanism (recent infection, high IgM). case_prompt: A 46‑year‑old man with a history of arterial hypertension and obesity was admitted to the intensive care unit for fever, hypotension, and marked asthenia. Two weeks earlier he had a mild COVID‑19 infection limited to rhinitis and cough. On admission he was alert, oriented, cooperative, and asthenic. Vital signs were: blood pressure 85/55 mmHg, heart rate ≈120 bpm, arterial oxygen saturation 85 % on room air, temperature 38.3 °C. A femoral central venous catheter was placed. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 122 bpm with diffuse low voltages and no significant repolarization abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 26 800/µL), CRP 17.4 mg/dL, procalcitonin 11.7 ng/mL, high‑sensitivity troponin 23 000 ng/L, BNP 6 890 pg/mL, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, and abnormal transaminases and total bilirubin. Nasopharyngeal RT‑PCR for SARS‑CoV‑2 was negative, but COVID‑19 IgM antibodies were markedly elevated. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated normal left‑ventricular dimensions but new diffuse LV wall thickening (15–16 mm) not present a few weeks earlier, extensive myocardial echogenicity, severely reduced LV ejection fraction (26 %), low cardiac index (1.3 L/min/m²), and grade II diastolic dysfunction. Right‑ventricular size was normal with reduced systolic function (TAPSE 14 mm, tricuspid S‑wave 7.3 cm/s). The inferior vena cava was dilated (26 mm) with <50 % inspiratory collapse. No significant valvular disease and a small pericardial effusion were noted. Thoracic CT showed perivascular aortic and pulmonary adipose tissue imbibition; abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (daptomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam), crystalloid resuscitation, nasal cannula oxygen (4 L/min), and norepinephrine infusion (up to 0.9 µg/kg/min) were initiated with poor hemodynamic response. Levosimendan infusion was started (0.1 µg/kg/min) without bolus due to renal and hepatic impairment. Within 12 hours blood pressure rose to 100/60 mmHg and heart rate fell to 110 bpm; after 24 hours BP was 125/70 mmHg, HR 95 bpm, urine output 1800 mL, and repeat echocardiography showed marked improvement of LV ejection fraction to 66 % and of RV function (TAPSE 23 mm, tricuspid S‑wave 11.2 cm/s). Inflammatory markers remained unchanged. Blood cultures and the tip culture of the removed central venous catheter later returned negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Septic shock was considered given fever, hypotension, and leukocytosis, but cultures were sterile, making infection unlikely | "Blood culture results were available, all negative."
2. Cardiogenic shock due to acute coronary syndrome was entertained because of troponin elevation and low EF; coronary angiography later showed normal arteries, excluding ischemia | "coronary arteriography, which showed normal coronary circulation."
3. Post‑COVID‑19 immune‑mediated myocarditis was hypothesized because of recent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection and high IgM levels despite negative PCR | "Two weeks prior... a COVID‑19 infection... occurred" and "COVID‑19 IgM antibody test was performed resulting in high IgM levels."
4. Primary viral myocarditis unrelated to COVID‑19 was a differential, but the temporal association with recent infection and lack of other viral serologies directed focus toward a post‑infectious immune mechanism. | (implicit from case narrative; no direct quote available).
5. Drug‑induced myocardial depression was less likely as no new cardiotoxic agents were introduced prior to presentation. | (implicit; no direct quote).

case_prompt:
A 72‑year‑old woman with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, prior thyroidectomy, and osteoporosis received the first dose of the mRNA COVID‑19 vaccine BNT162b2. Within one week she developed a persistent fever, which was followed over the next weeks by progressive shortness of breath, sore throat, polyarthralgia, malaise, decreased appetite, and insomnia. Empirical antibiotics and NSAIDs administered at another hospital did not relieve her symptoms.

Four weeks after vaccination she presented to our emergency department. On examination she was febrile (38.7 °C), blood pressure 100/72 mmHg, heart rate 162 beats/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air. Auscultation revealed bilateral basal crepitations. ECG showed atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response of 150–160 beats/min without ST‑segment or T‑wave changes. Laboratory studies demonstrated troponin T 7 000 ng/mL, B‑type natriuretic peptide >26 000 pg/mL, white blood cell count 20.44 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 19.06 × 10⁹/L), C‑reactive protein 22.4 ng/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 28 mm/h, AST 112 U/L and ALT 116 U/L. Chest X‑ray showed pulmonary congestion; thoracic CT was unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 16–20 % with global hypokinesia, moderate mitral regurgitation, and tricuspid regurgitation; no pericardial effusion was seen. Coronary angiography demonstrated no obstructive coronary artery disease. Endomyocardial biopsy of the right ventricular septum was non‑diagnostic. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed increased native T1 relaxation time and high T2 signal intensity, meeting the Lake Louise criteria for myocarditis. An extensive infectious work‑up (serology, PCR, cultures from blood, urine, stool, throat, nasopharyngeal swab, and other fluids) failed to identify a pathogen, and the patient was labeled as having vaccination‑induced myocarditis. She received diuretics, amiodarone, and apixaban. During hospitalization she experienced a brief episode of shock requiring norepinephrine and high‑flow oxygen, which stabilized after rate control.

Despite hemodynamic improvement, she continued to have high fever, polyarthralgia, leukocytosis, and elevated CRP. Ferritin was markedly elevated at 68 913 pmol/L. A diffuse, non‑itchy, salmon‑pink macular rash appeared predominantly on the trunk with some limb involvement. Autoantibody screening—including antinuclear antibody, anti‑double‑stranded DNA, anti‑extractable nuclear antigens, and rheumatoid factor—was negative. PET‑CT demonstrated lymphadenopathy in cervical, bilateral axillary, mediastinal, hilar, porta hepatis, and peripancreatic regions (SUVmax 4.7) but revealed no evidence of malignancy, infection, or systemic sarcoidosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Vaccine‑associated myocarditis diagnosed by CMR (Lake Louise criteria) and absence of coronary obstruction | "Myocarditis was diagnosed according to the Lake Louise criteria."
2. Infectious myocarditis ruled out by comprehensive microbiologic testing with no pathogen identified | "After an extensive search, no infective foci were identified; she was labeled as having vaccination-induced myocarditis."
3. Ischemic cardiac injury excluded by normal coronary angiography | "Coronary angiography revealed no obstructive coronary artery disease."
4. Autoimmune connective‑tissue disease (e.g., systemic lupus, rheumatoid arthritis) considered but excluded by negative ANA, anti‑dsDNA, ENA panel, and rheumatoid factor | "Autoantibody screening, including antinuclear antibody, anti‑double stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA), anti‑extractable nuclear antigens (anti-ENA), and rheumatoid factor, were all negative."
5. Malignancy and sarcoidosis evaluated with PET‑CT; lymphadenopathy present but no metabolic pattern of cancer or sarcoidosis | "Positron emission tomography and computed tomography (PET-CT) showed ... No malignancy, infective foci, or systemic feature of sarcoidosis was found."
6. Adult‑Onset Still’s disease considered after persistent fever, polyarthralgia, salmon‑pink rash, markedly elevated ferritin, and exclusion of infection, malignancy, and other autoimmune diseases; Yamaguchi criteria met (≥4 major, ≥2 minor) | "Subsequent review ... reached a diagnosis of AOSD based on the fulfillment of at least eight Yamaguchi criteria, including four major criteria, and after exclusion of infectious, malignant, and other autoimmune conditions."

case_prompt: A 48‑year‑old man presented to the outpatient department with pain and swelling in the right maxillary front tooth region. He had been hospitalized for COVID‑19 and discharged one month earlier. Extraoral examination revealed swelling over the right lip extending from the lateral nose to the mouth corner with mild nasolabial fold obliteration; the swelling was mildly tender and there were no palpable lymph nodes. Eye movements were normal, pupils reactive, and a nasal twang was noted in his voice. Intraorally, teeth #12 and #13 showed class 3 mobility, mild vestibular tenderness, and a soft, fluctuant swelling. Panoramic imaging demonstrated advanced bone loss around these teeth and an ill‑defined radiolucency in the right anterior maxillary alveolar bone extending to the floor of the right maxillary sinus, suggesting sinus involvement. A provisional diagnosis of periodontal abscess for teeth #12 and #13 was made. The clinician noted nasal twang, recent COVID‑19 infection, and bony changes in the sinus floor, and ordered magnetic resonance imaging. MRI showed mucosal thickening with T2‑hypointense components, non‑enhancement of the involved mucosa/soft tissue suggestive of a fungal aetiology in the right maxillary sinus, and hyperdensity of the maxillary antrum.

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s ultimate diagnosis is AIH‑PBC‑OS (autoimmune hepatitis‑primary biliary cholangitis overlap syndrome), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list; the earlier SARS‑CoV‑2 infection is a SELECTED disease but is presented only as a past infection without a diagnostic work‑up for the current problem. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation immediately before the sentence “According to the Paris Criteria (Table 2), the patient was diagnosed with AIH‑PBC‑OS…”. All data needed to reason toward an autoimmune hepatitis–primary biliary cholangitis overlap (antibody profile, histology, response to steroids, cholestatic pattern) are included, but the explicit diagnostic label is omitted.

case_prompt: A 45‑year‑old man presented with fever, cough, and body aches and was diagnosed with SARS‑CoV‑2 infection by RT‑PCR. His illness was mild, managed outpatient with loratadine, acetaminophen, and azithromycin for 5 days, and he recovered fully. Two weeks later he complained of weakness, jaundice, and pruritus, without fever. He denied recent travel, alcohol, herbal products, or illicit drug use. Physical examination revealed jaundice; no stigmata of chronic liver disease or lymphadenopathy were noted. Laboratory studies showed a cholestatic pattern of acute hepatitis with markedly elevated liver enzymes, total and direct bilirubin, and ferritin; INR, albumin, and γ‑globulin were unchanged. Renal function was impaired but later normalized; complement levels, creatine kinase, and urinalysis were normal. Serologies for hepatitis A‑E, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein‑Barr virus, and toxoplasmosis were negative. Autoimmune serology was positive for ANA (1:1280, nuclear fine speckled) and ASMA (1:160); AMA, anti‑dsDNA, and anti‑LKM1 were negative. A repeat SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR was negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a finely heterogeneous liver with thin borders and a regular surface; magnetic resonance cholangiography demonstrated normal biliary ducts. Because a specific diagnosis was lacking, an ultrasound‑guided percutaneous liver biopsy was performed, revealing acute/subacute hepatitis with numerous lobular necrotic foci, moderate canalicular and intrahepatocytic cholestasis (predominantly zone 3), without ductopenia or portal biliary reaction. The patient was started on oral prednisone 40 mg/day for 7 days with symptomatic improvement, then tapered to 30 mg/day for another week and subsequently to 20 mg/day. Liver enzymes rose again, prompting a second liver biopsy two months later. This biopsy showed non‑suppurative destructive chronic cholangitis, extensive confluent necrosis with hepatocyte regeneration into pseudorosettes, and numerous plasma cells.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Drug‑induced liver injury considered due to recent azithromycin and loratadine use, but histology showed cholestatic hepatitis without typical eosinophilic infiltrates or granulomas; “first liver biopsy showed acute/subacute hepatitis … without ductopenia or portal biliary reaction.” |
2. Acute viral hepatitis considered; serologies for hepatitis viruses, HIV, CMV, EBV, and toxoplasmosis were negative, leading to exclusion: “Serologies for viral hepatitis, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein‑Barr virus, and toxoplasmosis were unremarkable.” |
3. Autoimmune hepatitis (type 1) considered because of high ANA and ASMA titers; however, lack of response to steroids alone and negative anti‑LKM1 made isolated AIH less likely: “ANA and ASMA were positive … anti‑LKM1 were both negative.” |
4. Primary biliary cholangitis considered due to cholestatic picture, but AMA was negative and imaging showed normal biliary ducts: “anti‑mitochondrial antibody (AMA) … were both negative … magnetic resonance cholangiography showed normal biliary ducts.” |
5. Overlap syndrome (AIH‑PBC) considered when second biopsy revealed features of both AIH (plasma‑cell infiltrates, hepatocyte pseudorosettes) and PBC (non‑suppurative chronic cholangitis): “Liver histologic analysis revealed non‑suppurative destructive chronic cholangitis … numerous plasma cells.” |
6. Other differentials such as ischemic hepatitis or sepsis‑related cholestasis were excluded by normal hemodynamics, lack of hypotension, and absence of systemic infection signs: “Renal function exams normalized without the need for dialysis; no fever at second presentation.” |

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The case’s central diagnostic challenge is Pediatric Inflammatory Multisystem Syndrome temporally associated with SARS‑CoV‑2 (PIMS‑TS), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. The only SELECTED disease mentioned (SARS‑CoV‑2) is a prior infection, not the mystery syndrome itself. Therefore, the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Stop the narrative just before the authors state, “We diagnosed PIMS‑TS…”. Include all presenting signs (fever, cough, chest pain, neck pain, lymphadenopathy, elevated CRP, neutrophilia, lymphopenia, low vitamin D, elevated pro‑BNP, mild coronary dilation, pericardial effusion, MAP drop) and the initial negative infectious work‑up. Exclude the diagnostic declaration and subsequent treatment details.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out common bacterial (negative strep A) and viral (CMV, EBV, adenovirus) infections, demonstrated unremarkable CSF, and highlighted a recent SARS‑CoV‑2 exposure with positive IgG. Multisystem inflammation (cardiac, hematologic, gastrointestinal) together with the laboratory pattern led them to label the condition PIMS‑TS.
case_prompt: Patient 2, an 8‑year‑old girl, was admitted with a 3‑day history of fever up to 39 °C, dry cough, chest pain, headache, and neck pain. Physical examination revealed cervical lymphadenopathy, suspected meningism, and tonsillar swelling. A rapid streptococcal A test performed in the emergency department was negative. Anthropometry placed height at the 91st percentile, weight at the 80th percentile, and BMI at the 63rd percentile. During fever spikes the pulse was elevated and blood pressure was subnormal. Lung and heart auscultation were regular; the abdomen was mildly distended but ultrasound showed no hepatosplenomegaly. Skin examination showed only discrete palmar erythema without lesions. The child appeared generally ill. Laboratory studies demonstrated a C‑reactive protein up to 243 mg/L, neutrophilia (84 % of leukocytes) with concomitant lymphopenia (low 15 %), and a vitamin D₃ level of 14 nmol/L. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was unremarkable. A known exposure to SARS‑CoV‑2 was reported approximately three weeks earlier. Initial echocardiography showed a borderline ejection fraction; pro‑BNP was markedly elevated at 15 960 ng/L. Subsequent imaging documented mild dilatation of the coronary arteries (3–4 mm) and a small pericardial effusion, while the ejection fraction normalized. Mean arterial pressure was reduced by 46 mmHg. The patient had no prior medical conditions, medications, or psychosocial issues.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute streptococcal infection considered but excluded by a negative rapid test. | "The strep A test was negative in the emergency room."
2. Other viral infections (CMV, EBV, adenovirus) evaluated and ruled out. | "We excluded other causes of infections like potential bacterial and virus infections, e.g., cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and adenovirus."
3. Central nervous system infection (meningitis/encephalitis) considered; CSF findings normal. | "Cerebrospinal fluid results were unremarkable."
4. Primary bacterial sepsis considered given high fever and neutrophilia, but lack of focal infection, negative strep test, and absence of organ‑specific bacterial markers made it unlikely. | (implied by negative infectious work‑up and sterile CSF).
5. Post‑infectious hyperinflammatory syndrome (PIMS‑TS) favoured because of multisystem involvement (cardiac changes, elevated pro‑BNP, coronary dilation, pericardial effusion), marked inflammatory markers (CRP, neutrophilia, lymphopenia), and recent SARS‑CoV‑2 exposure with positive IgG antibodies. | "We diagnosed PIMS-TS according to patients' symptoms and laboratory parameters, such as elevated CRP, neutrophilia and lymphopenia... and especially positive SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH), which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best breakpoint: Include presentation from initial fever, COVID-19 diagnosis, admission vitals, initial normal labs (except ferritin), negative infectious work‑up, autoimmune and malignancy screening, and the early signs of clinical deterioration (new fever spikes, cognitive change, evolving cytopenias, rising ferritin, low fibrinogen, decreased NK activity, bone‑marrow hemophagocytosis) **up to but not including** the explicit statement “A diagnosis of sHLH was made…”.
3. Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors ruled out bacterial, mycobacterial, fungal, and viral infections; excluded malignancy by PET‑CT and marrow biopsy; evaluated autoimmune disease with serologies; documented persistent SARS‑CoV‑2 negativity; and highlighted the combination of fever, cytopenias, hyper‑ferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, low NK‑cell activity and hemophagocytosis that satisfied HLH‑2004 criteria, leading to the sHLH diagnosis.
case_prompt:
A 76‑year‑old man presented with three days of persistent fever without cough, sore throat, fatigue, or myalgia. He tested antigen‑positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 on 16 December 2022 during the Omicron wave, did not receive antivirals, and self‑treated with antipyretics for one day. His temperature normalized over the next half‑month, with loss of appetite as the main complaint, but fever recurred on 3 January 2023, prompting admission on 5 January 2023. He denied cough, sputum, hemoptysis, abdominal pain, diarrhea, arthralgia, erythema, environmental or occupational exposures, and long‑term drug use. Past history included hypertension; he denied autoimmune disease.

On admission he was clinically stable: SpO₂ 98 % on room air, HR 68 bpm, RR 18 /min, temperature 37.5 °C, BP 134/81 mmHg. Initial labs showed normal CBC, liver and renal panels, coagulation profile, and inflammatory markers except an elevated ferritin (480.2 µg/L; normal 23.9‑336.2). Repeated SARS‑CoV‑2 nasopharyngeal swabs every three days were negative. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, or fungi. Two next‑generation sequencing assays of peripheral blood were negative. Viral panels for CMV, HIV, hepatotropic viruses, HSV, influenza, parvovirus, adenovirus, and atypical respiratory pathogens were all negative. EBV DNA in peripheral‑blood lymphocytes was 1,780 copies/mL (normal < 500), but plasma EBV DNA and EBV‑IgM were negative. PET‑CT and bone‑marrow aspiration/biopsy showed no malignant lesions. Ultrasound did not reveal hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Serum tumor markers, immunofixation electrophoresis, superficial lymph‑node ultrasound, and head MRI were unremarkable except for a persistently elevated carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA 21 ng/mL, similar to prior 25.7 ng/mL). Rheumatologic work‑up showed a 1:320 ANA, 1:100 anti‑dsDNA, and mildly low C3 (0.546 g/L); anti‑ENA, antiphospholipid antibodies, direct Coombs, ANCA, and rheumatoid factor were negative.

During hospitalization his fever escalated to 39.8 °C and his mental status declined. Laboratory trends showed decreasing leukocytes, hemoglobin, and platelets; ferritin rose further; liver enzymes increased; fibrinogen fell; and natural killer cell activity was reduced. Bone‑marrow aspiration demonstrated hemophagocytosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection was excluded because “SARS‑Cov‑2 nasopharyngeal swabs were performed every three days and all of the tests were negative.”  
2. Bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal sepsis were ruled out as “Multiple cultures sets of blood, urine, and sputum were negative for bacteria, mycobacteria, or fungi.”  
3. Other viral etiologies were excluded: “Viral infections (CMV, human immunodeficiency virus, hepatotropic viruses, herpes simplex virus, influenza virus, parvovirus, adenovirus and atypical respiratory pathogens) were promptly ruled out.”  
4. EBV primary infection was unlikely given the pattern: “EBV‑DNA in peripheral blood lymphocytes was 1780 copies/mL … EBV‑DNA in plasma and EBV‑IgM antibody were negative.”  
5. Malignancy was not supported: “No signs of malignant lesions were found in positron emission tomography‑computed tomography (PET‑CT) or bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.”  
6. Connective‑tissue disease (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus) was considered but not confirmed: “Rheumatologic tests showed the 1:320 positive antinuclear antibody, 1:100 positive anti‑dsDNA antibody … Other indications of connective tissue disease … were all negative.”  
7. Drug‑induced fever or hypersensitivity reaction was unlikely because “There was no history of environmental, occupational or long‑term drug exposure.”  
8. The constellation of fever, cytopenias, hyper‑ferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, low NK‑cell activity, and hemophagocytosis satisfied HLH‑2004 criteria, leading to the diagnosis of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

The case provides sufficient clinical and laboratory data to deduce both, but the confirmation of COVID‑19 (RT‑PCR positive) occurs later in the report. I will set the target diagnosis as **covid_19**, using the early presentation and subsequent work‑up to allow students to arrive at this diagnosis before the test result is disclosed.

On examination she was lethargic, mildly jaundiced, and pale. She had mild epigastric tenderness; no abdominal organ was palpable. Vital signs: temperature 37.8 °C, pulse 109 beats/min, blood pressure normal, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies revealed a malaria parasite density of 600,000 /µL, reduced hemoglobin, thrombocytopenia, and normal renal function.

She was diagnosed with severe malaria with thrombocytopenia and anemia and started on intravenous artesunate (125 mg at 0, 12, and 24 h) followed by oral artemether‑lumefantrine. Paracetamol 1 g IV every 8 h was given for fever. Within 12 hours her temperature rose to 39 °C, blood pressure fell to 68/38 mmHg, and she developed respiratory distress (respiratory rate 35 /min, flaring of the nares). Oxygen saturation on room air dropped to 45%. The working impression was severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with a differential of septic shock, acute asthma exacerbation, and possible COVID‑19. She was positioned at 45°, given 10 L/min oxygen via a non‑rebreather mask, intravenous fluids, nebulized salbutamol (5 mg ×3), and IV hydrocortisone 200 mg. Oxygen saturation improved to 75–77% on oxygen, blood pressure rose to 132/78 mmHg, and respiratory rate remained at 40 /min. Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and continued salbutamol nebulizations were initiated.

On day 3 of admission dyspnea improved, temperature fell to 37 °C, pulse 111 beats/min, and oxygen saturation reached 96% on the non‑rebreather mask with the patient propped at 45°. Chest X‑ray showed heterogeneous opacifications in the upper right lung zones and homogeneous opacifications in the lower lung zones. Repeat malaria blood film showed a reduced parasite load, and ESR rose to 100 mm / hr.

On day 4 temperature was 36.7 °C, pulse 132 beats/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 91% on oxygen. The impression remained severe malaria complicated by thrombocytopenia, intravascular hemolysis, and ARDS with a differential of COVID‑19. Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs were collected for COVID‑19 testing, and azithromycin 500 mg was started, followed by a tapering course of dexamethasone, zinc, and vitamin C.

On day 5 the patient reported no new complaints. Vital signs: temperature 37.2 °C, pulse 83 beats/min, blood pressure 89/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min off oxygen and 26 /min on oxygen. Oxygen saturation was 82–84% off oxygen and 96–97% on a non‑rebreather mask at 10 L/min. Examination of other systems was unremarkable, and all medications were continued.

3. Acute asthma exacerbation – Known asthmatic history, wheezes on exam, and need for nebulized salbutamol supported this possibility; “…acute exacerbation of asthma…”

5. Bacterial superinfection – Empiric ceftriaxone was started, reflecting concern for bacterial pneumonia; “The patient was started on intravenous ceftriaxone 2g daily…”
6. Drug‑induced hemolysis – Intravascular hemolysis was noted as a complication of severe malaria, not a separate diagnosis; “…intravascular hemolysis…”

case_prompt:
The participant, Ms X, was a 49‑year‑old South African citizen with no known medical history, living and working in a Middle‑East country. In late March 2020, travel visas were revoked and an evacuation flight was arranged for stranded South Africans. After return to South Africa, participants were taken to a government site in Johannesburg for a mandatory 14‑day quarantine. Ms X was assigned a 4 × 4 m² room with bed and amenities; meals and drinks were provided. Military and police personnel ensured confinement to rooms, and medical staff monitored general health.

Nasal and oropharyngeal samples for COVID‑19 detection were collected by on‑call laboratory staff. Testing could be performed only in the latter part of quarantine; Ms X was tested on Day 14.

On Day 1 Ms X self‑reported height 1.65 m and weight 68 kg. She measured waist and hip circumferences daily, calculated BMI (kg/m²) and waist‑to‑height ratio (WHtR). Daily dietary intake and beverage consumption were recorded and converted to macronutrients using an online calculator. The short‑form health survey (SF‑36) was completed online to assess physical and mental health. Night‑time sleep hours and estimated sitting time per day were also recorded.

Ms X followed online moderate‑to‑vigorous home‑based exercise videos (continuous aerobic activity, high‑intensity interval training, and body‑weight resistance training). A wireless heart‑rate monitor was worn during exercise; peak and average heart rate, calories expended, and exercise intensity (% max) were monitored in real time on a smartphone app and saved to a cloud platform. Step count and stepping duration were recorded using the iPhone Health app.

Ms X remained asymptomatic throughout quarantine. Her height and weight remained unchanged; BMI was 25.0 kg/m² (overweight). Waist circumference was 82 cm, hip circumference 102 cm, and WHtR 0.497 (just below the cut‑point for abdominal obesity). The average resting heart rate was 63.8 b/min (range 58–73), and average night‑time sleep was 8.4 h/night. Caloric intake fluctuated, with peaks of 1 617–2 854 kcal/day. Most energy came from carbohydrates (≈40‑54 % of total), followed by fats (25‑45 %) and proteins (15‑25 %). Added sugars contributed 4.4‑12.5 % of energy. Quality‑of‑life scores were initially low and improved toward the end of quarantine.

Physical activity was not performed every day. Total sitting time averaged 516 min/day (7‑10 h). Stepping time ranged from 20‑49 min/day. Ten exercise sessions were completed, with an average effort of 71.8 % per session (range 62‑81 %), average duration 46.9 min (range 15‑75 min), and average caloric expenditure 366 kcal per session (range 79‑591 kcal). Total physical‑activity time over 14 days was 7.82 h, performed at moderate intensity via the mobile application.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 infection was the primary concern due to exposure during evacuation and quarantine, but the participant remained asymptomatic and a PCR test performed on Day 14 was negative, ruling out active infection. | "Ms X remained asymptomatic and tested negative for COVID-19 on Day 14."
2. No other infectious disease was reported or investigated in the article; the absence of symptoms, normal vital signs, and lack of laboratory abnormalities further excluded alternative acute illnesses. | "Ms X remained asymptomatic..."

case_prompt: A 39‑year‑old woman with a past history of steroid‑responsive bilateral optic neuritis in 2010 and subsequent unilateral episodes in 2016 and 2018 was diagnosed with MOG‑IgG1 antibody‑positive disease (MOGAD). She had been treated with mycophenolate mofetil 2 g/day and low‑dose prednisolone; serologic testing remained positive for >3.5 years before the antibodies fell below the cutoff and became negative. After tapering steroids completely, four months later she developed malaise, coryzal symptoms, sweating, and postural dizziness. A nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR, confirming COVID‑19. Six days after the positive test she complained of pain on right eye movement and worsening vision. On admission she had a right relative afferent pupillary defect and visual acuity reduced to hand movements in the right eye; left eye visual acuity was 6/6. The remainder of the cranial nerve exam was normal, with no pyramidal signs, and sensory, gait, and coordination examinations were unremarkable. Admission laboratory studies—including complete blood count, renal and liver panels, C‑reactive protein—and chest radiography were all within normal limits. Brain and cervical spinal MRI performed previously had shown no demyelination. Cross‑sectional imaging of the brain and orbits was not obtained during the acute illness because of concern for SARS‑CoV‑2 transmission.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Prior MOG‑IgG1 seropositivity established a predisposition to MOGAD relapse | "She tested positive for serum MOG‑IgG1 antibodies by live cell‑based assay after her second relapse, confirming a diagnosis of MOGAD…" 
2. Normal brain and cervical cord MRI with no demyelination argued against multiple sclerosis or NMOSD | "MRI appearances of the brain and cervical cord were normal with no evidence of demyelination."
3. Absence of oligoclonal bands in CSF further reduced the likelihood of multiple sclerosis | "Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was acellular with normal protein and absence of unmatched oligoclonal bands…"
4. Normal inflammatory markers and chest X‑ray made a systemic infectious or inflammatory cause unlikely | "Admission work‑up including hematological, renal, liver parameters, C‑reactive protein, and chest x‑ray were normal."
5. COVID‑19 infection could cause optic neuropathy, but the rapid, severe visual loss and relative afferent pupillary defect are classic for demyelinating optic neuritis rather than a viral optic neuropathy | "Based on systemic symptoms and a SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR positive nasopharyngeal swab, COVID‑19 was confirmed… On admission, consistent with optic neuritis she had a right relative afferent pupillary defect…"
6. The return of visual symptoms after a period of antibody negativity suggested seroreversion rather than a new unrelated process | (implied by the clinical course described prior to the serology result).

case_prompt:
A 21‑year‑old otherwise healthy female presented with a 10‑day history of high‑grade fever, dry cough, and anosmia, followed by an acute onset (over a few hours) of flaccid paralysis and numbness of both lower limbs with difficulty voiding. One day later she developed weakness and numbness of both upper limbs with urinary and fecal retention. Autonomic symptoms included heart‑rate fluctuations, frequent palpitations, and dizziness/fainting on sitting. No recent vaccinations and no prior similar episodes were reported.

On exam, heart sounds were normal, blood pressure was symmetrical, and the neurologic exam revealed quadriplegia (more severe in the lower limbs), areflexia, bilateral Babinski signs, loss of pain and temperature sensation up to the C4 level, with preserved touch, vibration, and joint‑position sense.

Laboratory studies showed a positive SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR, elevated D‑dimer (4.6 mg/L) and ferritin (502 ng/mL), neutrophilia (85.7 %), lymphopenia (17 %), anemia (Hb 10.8 g/dL), markedly elevated ESR (100‑150 mm/hr), CRP (111 mg/dL), and LDH (356 U/L). Electrolytes, coagulation profile, and complete blood count otherwise were within normal limits. Visual and brain‑stem auditory evoked potentials were normal. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground‑glass opacities without evidence of aortic dissection. MRI of the spine revealed an extensive hyperintense T2 signal from C5 to T7, involving the anterior two‑thirds of the cord, affecting both gray and white matter, with mild cord swelling.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of anterior spinal artery occlusion based on extensive anterior cord involvement and clinical pattern | "The possibility of anterior spinal artery occlusion was considered given the clinical presentation, laboratory, and MRI findings."
2. Multiple sclerosis deemed unlikely because of long segment anterior cord lesion, normal evoked potentials, and lack of brain lesions | "Given her age, multiple sclerosis was considered as a possible diagnosis. However, the long segment of cord involvement, together with the normal evoked potentials and no positive MRI findings in the brain, excluded multiple sclerosis."
3. Transverse myelitis considered but deep sensation preservation favored vascular etiology | "The possibility of transverse myelitis was also considered as a differential diagnosis of long segment myelopathy; however, the complete preservation of deep sensation on clinical examination could support the diagnosis of anterior spinal artery occlusion."
4. Aortic dissection ruled out due to normal chest CT and symmetrical arm blood pressures | "A CT of the chest showed no evidence of aortic dissection with normal heart and symmetrical blood pressure in both arms. Thus, we think it unlikely that the lesion was the result of aortic dissection-related occlusion of multiple supplying arteries."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The case’s primary mystery is the cause of the NSTEMI and need for emergent CABG. The only disease from the 21 SELECTED list mentioned is covid_19, but it is already known at admission and not the focus of diagnostic work‑up. Therefore the target diagnosis is the out‑of‑scope entity that the authors ultimately identified – coronary artery dissection.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the prompt after the coronary angiogram description (critical stenoses of LAD, OM, sub‑occlusion of LCx) and before any mention of the intravascular ultrasound findings that reveal the dissection. This gives sufficient clinical, laboratory, and imaging data (COVID‑19 positivity, NSTEMI, multivessel disease) for learners to generate a differential and arrive at the final diagnosis without explicit spoilers.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors diagnosed NSTEMI by ECG and troponin rise, excluded systemic inflammation (normal inflammatory markers), identified multivessel critical stenoses on angiography, then used IVUS which demonstrated an arterial dissection that precluded successful PCI, leading to emergency CABG. The dissection was distinguished from atherosclerotic plaque rupture or thrombotic occlusion by the direct IVUS visualization of a dissected vessel.
case_prompt: A 57‑year‑old woman with a history of smoking, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and hypothyroidism tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 and was receiving azithromycin and enoxaparin. She was admitted for chest pain. Laboratory studies on admission showed elevated LDH and a high‑sensitivity cardiac troponin T of 0.156 µg/dL (peaking at 0.348 µg/dL). Inflammatory markers were not elevated. An electrocardiogram demonstrated findings consistent with a non‑ST‑elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Chest computed tomography revealed bilateral ground‑glass opacities without pleural or pericardial effusion. Coronary angiography showed critical stenosis of the left anterior descending artery and the first obtuse marginal artery, and sub‑occlusion of the left circumflex artery.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Atherosclerotic coronary artery disease causing NSTEMI | "critical stenosis of both left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery and first obtuse marginal (OM) coronary artery, and sub‑occlusion of left circumflex (LCx) coronary artery."
2. COVID‑19‑related hypercoagulability leading to thrombotic coronary occlusion | "No inflammatory markers elevations associated with COVID‑19 were found," suggesting that systemic inflammation was not the primary driver.
3. Myocarditis mimicking NSTEMI in COVID‑19 | "No inflammatory markers elevations associated with COVID‑19 were found," arguing against an inflammatory myocardial process.
4. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) as the underlying cause of the angiographic findings | "During intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) study, OM coronary artery was dissected…" confirming the presence of a dissection that explained the failure of percutaneous coronary intervention.

case_prompt:
A 47‑year‑old man with hypertension was admitted for COVID‑19 confirmed by RT‑PCR. Ten days after diagnosis he developed fever, a non‑productive cough, and progressive dyspnea. On hospital day 4 he required ICU admission for worsening oxygen saturation; a thoracic CT showed diffuse bilateral infiltrates with ground‑glass opacities, crazy‑paving, and lower‑lobe consolidation. While in the ICU he received subcutaneous heparin, IV prednisolone, IV moxifloxacin, oral favipiravir, and IV ceftriaxone.

On ICU day 2 he experienced typical anginal chest pain. Vital signs while on high‑flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) were: blood pressure 135/68 mm Hg, heart rate 73 bpm, SpO₂ 88‑93 % on 60 L/min, FiO₂ 90 %, temperature 36.7 °C. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. A 12‑lead ECG demonstrated inferior ST‑segment elevation consistent with STEMI. He was given 300 mg oral aspirin, 180 mg oral ticagrelor, and IV heparin (4,000 IU). Chest pain resolved within 30 minutes.

Emergency coronary angiography revealed 30‑40 % stenosis in the mid‑LAD; the left main, left circumflex, and right coronary arteries appeared normal. High‑sensitivity troponin I measured at the time of pain was 0.012 ng/mL (reference < 0.0262 ng/mL) and rose to 0.056 ng/mL after the procedure. Renal and liver panels were normal. Inflammatory markers were elevated: D‑dimer 520 ng/mL (N < 500), fibrinogen 589 mg/dL (N 200‑400), ferritin 1,693 ng/mL (N 22‑275), LDH 466 U/L (N 125‑220), CRP 4.1 mg/dL (N < 0.5). Pro‑BNP was 20 pg/mL (N < 100). Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography showed no pulmonary embolism.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Obstructive coronary artery disease (typical STEMI) was considered but excluded because angiography demonstrated only mild (30‑40 %) stenosis in the mid‑LAD and otherwise normal coronary arteries. | "Emergency coronary angiography showed 30‑40% stenosis in the midportion of the left anterior descending artery. In addition to this, the left main coronary artery, left circumflex artery and right coronary artery were observedly normal."
2. Pulmonary embolism as a cause of chest pain and troponin elevation was ruled out by imaging. | "CTPA did not reveal any evidence of pulmonary embolism."
3. Myocardial infarction with non‑obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) was supported by the presence of inferior STEMI on ECG, transient chest pain, modest troponin rise, absence of significant coronary obstruction, and cardiogoniometry indicating septal inferior myocardial ischemia. | "MINOCA was considered in the patient whose ECG findings showed inferior STEMI at the time of typical angina pain while his coronary angiography did not reveal any sign of significant stenosis."

case_prompt:
A 14‑year‑old teenager with moderate obesity (BMI 31 kg/m²) presented with NYHA class IV dyspnea and sudden chest pain. Three weeks prior she had an influenza‑like syndrome, dry cough, and exertional dyspnea. Her parents were being treated for COVID‑19. She had received antibiotics, oral corticosteroids, and inhaled bronchodilators from her general practitioner, but dyspnea worsened, accompanied by palpitations and chest pain.

On examination she was pale, anxious, afebrile, tachycardic (125 bpm), blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, SpO₂ 90% on room air. Cardiac auscultation revealed regular tachycardia without murmur; there were no signs of right or left heart failure and no evidence of deep‑vein thrombosis.

Laboratory tests showed a normal complete blood count and coagulation profile, markedly elevated D‑dimer (3520 ng FEU/ml), an inflammatory syndrome (ESR 28 mm, CRP 26 mg/L) with negative procalcitonin. Echocardiography demonstrated acute right‑heart strain with a very dilated right ventricle, a mass on the right‑ventricular lateral wall, pulmonary hypertension (50 mmHg) and a paradoxical septum, while systolic function of both ventricles was preserved. Chest CT angiography revealed bilateral massive pulmonary emboli without parenchymal lesions. Cardiac MRI confirmed that the right‑ventricular mass was thrombotic and excluded a tissue (tumoral) character; right‑ventricular systolic function remained preserved.

A comprehensive etiologic work‑up was performed. Venous Doppler ultrasound of the lower limbs and abdominal ultrasound were normal. Testing for inherited thrombophilia (protein C, protein S, antithrombin) and for autoimmune disease (anti‑cardiolipin IgM/IgG, ANA, anti‑DNA) were all negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Massive bilateral pulmonary embolism causing acute right‑heart strain – "CT angiogram of the chest showed a bilateral massive pulmonary embolism".
2. Right‑ventricular intracavitary thrombus rather than tumor – "MRI confirmed the thrombotic nature of the mass and eliminated its tissue character".
3. Inherited thrombophilia considered but excluded – "Biological assessment for thrombophilia (C protein, S protein, antithrombin) ... was negative".
4. Antiphospholipid/autoimmune hypercoagulability evaluated and ruled out – "anti‑cardiolipin antibody IgM and IgG, anti‑nuclear antibody, anti‑DNA antibody ... were negative".
5. Deep‑vein thrombosis as source of emboli investigated and not found – "venous Doppler of the lower limbs ... was normal".
6. Recent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection as a pro‑thrombotic trigger – "SARS‑CoV‑2 nasopharyngeal PCR was negative but SARS‑CoV‑2 antibody was positive (IgG)".

This provides sufficient clues (neurologic deterioration, ischemic‑appearing lesions, nonketotic hyperglycemia, negative bacterial cultures, EEG seizures) for the learner to consider SARS‑CoV‑2 encephalopathy without revealing the positive PCR.

case_prompt:
A 79‑year‑old man with a 10‑year history of type‑2 diabetes (on metformin) and 5‑year hypertension (on amlodipine) presented with acute mental confusion and dysarthria of 48 hours’ duration. On exam his Glasgow Coma Scale was 12/15 (E5 V2 M5), pupils were symmetric and reactive, no focal motor deficits were noted, and osteotendinous reflexes were normal. He was tachypneic (24 breaths/min), SpO₂ 97 % on room air, tachycardic (115 bpm) and hypertensive (160/95 mmHg). Capillary glucose was 2.24 g/L with glycosuria but no ketonuria. Arterial blood gas revealed a normal‑gap metabolic acidosis, potassium 3 mmol/L, lactate 0.43 mmol/L. He was afebrile.

Initial management addressed presumed diabetic decompensation with intravenous insulin, fluid resuscitation, and potassium correction. Because his neurological status did not improve, he was transferred to intensive care. Brain CT showed multiple parietal ischemic foci. Chest CT demonstrated septal thickening and bronchial dilatation without pneumonia typical of COVID‑19; abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable.

ECG showed no hypokalaemia‑related changes, transthoracic echocardiography and supra‑aortic trunk ultrasound were normal. Laboratory studies revealed CRP 45.5 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.04 ng/mL, leukocytes 12,500 /µL (neutrophils 9,280, lymphocytes 2,140), normal platelets, ferritin, fibrinogen 5.37 g/L, and negative D‑dimer. Electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and thyroid function were within normal limits. Nasopharyngeal SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR and IgM/IgG serology were negative.

Empiric therapy included prophylactic anticoagulation, aspirin, statin, and ceftriaxone at meningitis dosing pending lumbar puncture. CSF analysis showed clear fluid with elevated protein 0.58 g/L (reference 0.15–0.45 g/L), normal CSF‑to‑serum glucose ratio 0.58, and a sterile culture after 24 h. Cerebral MR angiography on day 2 demonstrated vascular leukopathy, basal ganglia calcifications, and cortical atrophy. EEG revealed epileptiform activity, leading to a provisional diagnosis of non‑ketotic hyperglycemia‑related seizures and initiation of sodium valproate.

Neurologic status continued to decline; he required intubation on day 3 (five days after symptom onset). Repeat brain CT showed no progression of lesions. New lymphopenia was noted, HIV serologies were negative, and CRP rose further. A multiplex RT‑PCR on a protected distal bronchial specimen and on CSF were ordered.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ischemic stroke considered due to acute focal neurologic signs and CT showing parietal hypodensities | "brain scan was performed objectifying multiple parietal ischemic foci".  
2. Bacterial meningitis evaluated because of encephalopathy; ruled out by sterile CSF culture and low white cell count in CSF | "CSF showed a clear liquid … culture showing less than 3 elements, sterile after 24 hours".  
3. Non‑ketotic hyperglycemia–related seizures proposed given severe hyperglycaemia without ketosis and EEG epileptiform activity | "Electroencephalogram showed signs of epilepsy, which prompted us to retain the diagnosis of nonketotic hyperglycemia-related epileptic seizures".  
4. Metabolic encephalopathy from diabetic decompensation addressed; ketones absent and metabolic acidosis mild, making it less likely as sole cause | "Diagnosis of diabetes decompensation was made despite absence of ketone bodies on urine dipstick test".  
5. Common viral encephalitides (e.g., HSV) considered but not supported by negative nasopharyngeal PCR and lack of typical CSF pleocytosis | "SARS‑CoV‑2 reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT‑PCR) by nasopharyngeal swab was negative, COVID‑19 serology (IgM and IgG) was also negative".  
6. COVID‑19 pneumonia initially deemed unlikely because chest CT lacked typical findings and nasopharyngeal PCR/serology were negative | "chest scanner showed a thickening of the septal and foci of bronchial dilation without sign of pneumopathy linked to COVID‑19 infection".  
7. SARS‑CoV‑2 encephalopathy ultimately diagnosed after detection of viral RNA in lower respiratory and CSF specimens, despite previous negative upper‑airway tests | "the first was positive to SARS‑CoV‑2. Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction of SARS‑CoV‑2 in CSF was positive but with a cycle threshold (CT) of 38.6".  
8. HIV infection excluded as a cause of lymphopenia and encephalopathy by negative serologies | "HIV serologies 1 and 2 negative".  
9. Sepsis unlikely given normal procalcitonin and absence of systemic infection signs | "CRP of 45.5 with negative procalcitonin (0.04 ng/ml)".

case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man with a past medical history of tobacco use, obesity (BMI 29 kg/m²), type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease was brought to the emergency department because of cough, fever, watery diarrhea, and altered mental status lasting five days. Nasopharyngeal swab testing was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by PCR, and he rapidly progressed to COVID‑19 pneumonia with acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring intubation. His hospital course was complicated by sepsis, acute kidney injury necessitating peritoneal dialysis, ileus, toxic metabolic encephalopathy, and candidemia (Candida tropicalis and Candida glabrata). 

On hospital day 40 he developed intermittent hematochezia requiring blood transfusion. Blood pressure varied from 138/69–175/80 mm Hg before the bleed and dropped to 118/49 mm Hg after passing large clots and dark‑red liquid blood. Laboratory parameters were notable for a falling hemoglobin (see Table 2). Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis showed a bowel of normal caliber without obstruction. He was on azithromycin, hydroxychloroquine, fluconazole, meropenem, micafungin, intravenous vancomycin, and ampicillin‑sulbactam at the time of bleeding; stool cultures were negative for cysts, ova, and parasites.

Colonoscopy identified patchy, deeply ulcerated mucosa with marked edema and loss of the vascular pattern in the cecum, extending to the ileocecal valve. Diffuse oozing of the mucosa was observed. The remaining colon appeared normal. No hemorrhoidal bleeding, arteriovenous malformation, diverticulitis, or overt mass lesions were identified.
diagnostic_reasoning:

Hemorrhoidal bleeding, AVM, diverticulitis, or colonic malignancy were considered but excluded because endoscopic evaluation showed ulcerated cecal lesions without hemorrhoids, vascular malformations, diverticula, or mass lesions. | "no evidence of hemorrhoidal bleeding, AVM, diverticulitis, and/or malignancy was noted."

case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old woman with diet‑controlled diabetes presented with a sudden, asymptomatic ecchymotic patch on her left lower limb. She denied any other medical problems or medications. On examination she was hemodynamically stable (BP 90/60 mmHg, RR 18, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.7 °C, SpO₂ 97%). Peripheral pulses were palpable bilaterally.  

During hospitalization the skin lesion evolved into hemorrhagic bullae with an erythematous border. The initial work‑up included complete blood count, metabolic panel, inflammatory markers, coagulation profile, and imaging. Laboratory results were: WBC 20 600 /µL (84.2 % neutrophils), platelets 137 000/µL, Hb 11.9 g/dL, IgA 475 mg/dL, IL‑6 60 pg/mL, amylase 145 U/L, pro‑BNP 297 pg/mL, ESR 41 mm/hr, LDH 983 U/L, PT 15.5 s, aPTT 30 s, INR 1.3, blood glucose 526 mg/dL. Liver enzymes, BUN, creatinine, CPK, troponin, and CRP were within normal limits. Urine and blood cultures (24‑h and 48‑h) showed no bacterial growth.  

Doppler ultrasound revealed an atheromatous plaque in the right common femoral artery; flow in the left lower limb was normal. A chest CT scan demonstrated bilateral peripheral ground‑glass opacities, more prominent in the lower lobes.  

Differential diagnoses considered for the skin lesion included necrotizing fasciitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation/purpura fulminans, drug‑induced necrosis, and vasculitis/vasculopathy secondary to rheumatologic disease or uncommon infections. The patient’s only systemic symptom during hospitalization was a fever of 38.8 °C that appeared one day after admission, accompanied by anorexia and nausea.

Lung examination revealed bilateral coarse crackles in the lower fields. Arterial blood gas showed pH 7.6, PaO₂ 42 mmHg, PaCO₂ 22 mmHg, consistent with hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis. She progressed to mild respiratory distress syndrome (PaO₂/FiO₂ 250) and required CPAP. After 18 days of hospitalization she improved, was discharged on room air with oxygen saturation 92% and a negative SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR.

Physical exam revealed elevated jugular venous pressure (13 cm H₂O), left parasternal heave, and wide splitting of the second heart sound. A repeat SARS‑CoV‑2 RT‑PCR was negative. Chest X‑ray showed right atrial enlargement and fibrotic changes. High‑resolution CT of the chest revealed extensive fibrosis, diffuse symmetrical ground‑glass opacities in both lungs, septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis, interpreted as post‑COVID‑19 lung disease. Electrocardiography demonstrated right‑axis deviation. Transthoracic echocardiography measured a right ventricular systolic pressure of 59 mmHg, tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity of 4.5 m/s, pulmonary artery diameter of 31 mm, and normal left‑heart parameters.

Pulmonary hypertension secondary to chronic lung disease post‑COVID‑19 considered; supported by HRCT findings of massive fibrosis, ground‑glass opacities, septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis consistent with post‑COVID‑19 changes. | “A high‑resolution CT‑scan revealed massive fibrosis, diffuse symmetrical ground glass opacities … most consistent with post‑COVID‑19 changes.”

case_prompt:

On hospital day 12 she experienced bouts of dizziness with nausea and was found to have systolic blood pressures in the high 70s to low 80s mm Hg. case_prompt:
A previously healthy 6‑year‑old boy presented to the emergency department after 10 days of fever. Five days earlier a SARS‑CoV‑2 infection had been confirmed by RT‑PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab. On admission he was febrile (39.8 °C), tachycardic (150 bpm), hypotensive (75/38 mmHg), tachypneic (50/min) and complained of abdominal pain. Chest radiography showed right lower‑lobe pneumonia with moderate pleural effusion. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly with ascites. Echocardiography revealed normal cardiac function and no coronary abnormalities. Laboratory studies showed anemia (Hb 108 g/L), thrombocytopenia (103 ×10⁹/L), normal neutrophil and lymphocyte counts, normal CRP, elevated ESR (36 mm/h) and ferritin (3 995 µg/L). Liver enzymes were markedly increased (ALT 511 U/L, bilirubin 75 µmol/L, GGT 396 U/L) with hypoalbuminemia (22 g/L). Hyponatremia (124 mmol/L) was present. Coagulation profile showed low fibrinogen (1.09 g/L) and high D‑dimer (6.4 mg/L). Troponin and NT‑pro‑BNP were normal. Multiplex PCR for respiratory viruses, including SARS‑CoV‑2, was negative on admission and SARS‑CoV‑2 antibodies were later absent.

The patient met diagnostic criteria for multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS‑C) and was transferred to intensive care. Empiric antibiotics were started; he developed acute respiratory distress with pulmonary edema, prompting treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) and methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day). After 24 h without improvement, an IL‑1 receptor antagonist (anakinra 8‑9 mg/kg/day subcutaneously) was added, but his condition continued to deteriorate. He then manifested liver failure, lactacidemia and profound coagulopathy, raising suspicion for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Consequently, anakinra was stopped and therapy with anti‑human‑T‑lymphocyte‑immunoglobulin (ATG) and cyclosporine was initiated. EBV PCR showed a very high viral load (20 ×10⁶ copies/mL); rituximab was added after these results became available. Despite supportive measures including a molecular adsorbent recirculation system, the patient’s condition worsened and he died on day 8 after admission.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. MIS‑C considered because the patient met established criteria (fever, laboratory inflammation, multisystem involvement) after recent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection | "The patient fulfilled the diagnostic criteria of MIS‑C at time of admission".
2. Secondary HLH suspected due to liver failure, lactacidemia, and severe coagulopathy, which are hallmark features of HLH | "He developed liver failure, lactacidemia and profound coagulopathy, highly suggestive of HLH".
3. EBV‑driven HLH evaluated because extremely high EBV DNA copies were detected in blood, indicating viral trigger | "Suspicion of primary HLH was something later strengthened by the detection of very high EBV copy numbers in the blood (20 × 10⁶ copies/mL)".
4. Primary (familial) HLH explored through immunologic assays showing normal NK‑cell degranulation (CD107a) and normal perforin expression, which argue against classic familial HLH mutations | "Immunological investigations on day 6 had shown normal CD107a expression in NK cell degranulation assay and normal intracellular perforin expression".
5. X‑linked lymphoproliferative syndrome type 1 (XLP1) ultimately identified by pathogenic SH2D1A mutation, explaining the severe EBV‑associated HLH and poor response to therapy | "However, an X‑linked mutation … in the SH2D1A gene was found, which has previously been described to be disease‑causing. Thus, the diagnosis of an X‑linked lymphoproliferative syndrome type 1 (XLP1) was made post‑mortem".

Pure COVID‑19‑related lung injury was plausible because of viral pneumonia on CT, but the presence of high‑titer p‑ANCA and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis pointed toward an ANCA‑associated vasculitis rather than isolated viral damage. | "p‑ANCA were found with a high titer (>200; N: <1:20), suggesting p‑ANCA vasculitis complicating COVID‑19"
