case_prompt:
An 18‑year‑old male presented to the emergency department with hyperpyrexia (42 °C), chills, and tachycardia. Physical examination and chest X‑ray were unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (105.9 mg/L) and interleukin‑6 (128 pg/mL) with only modestly raised procalcitonin (0.12 ng/mL). He was admitted to a standard care ward and started on empiric antibiotics.

Two months earlier he had been exposed to SARS‑CoV‑2 and experienced transient loss of smell; repeated nasopharyngeal swabs never confirmed active infection. Over the next three days his condition deteriorated, prompting transfer to the ICU for arterial hypotension with suspected septic shock. Fluid resuscitation and low‑dose norepinephrine stabilized his blood pressure. A generalized rash involving the abdomen and limbs appeared.

On day 4, transthoracic echocardiography revealed severe left‑ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF 25 %). Pulse contour cardiac output measurement showed marginal output (4.4 L/min). Computed tomography demonstrated enlarged abdominal lymph nodes, colonic wall thickening, polyserositis with pericardial and pleural effusions, and ascites. Respiratory failure due to pulmonary edema required non‑invasive ventilation.

That same day liver and renal failure and a massive systemic inflammatory response became evident. Rheumatologic workup (ANA, ENA, ANCA, antiphospholipid antibodies, complement) was unremarkable. Microbiologic testing identified only positive SARS‑CoV‑2 serology (anti‑S1 and anti‑N antibodies).

He was transferred to a tertiary center, where levosimendan infusion was initiated. Endomyocardial biopsy later showed infiltrates of CD68⁺ macrophages and CD3⁺ T cells around small vessels, with perivascular fibrosis but no myocyte necrosis. Nested (RT‑)PCR panels for enteroviruses, parvovirus B19, HHV‑6, EBV, adenovirus, CMV, HSV‑1/2, HHV‑7, VZV, influenza A/B, Toxoplasma gondii, and Borrelia spp. were negative in myocardial tissue and blood, and quantitative RT‑PCR did not detect SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA in the myocardium.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial septic shock considered due to hypotension, rash, and high CRP, but lack of microbiologic pathogen and modest procalcitonin made infection unlikely | "After 3 days he was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) due to arterial hypotension with suspected septic shock."
2. Autoimmune vasculitis or systemic rheumatologic disease entertained; extensive serologic panel (ANA, ENA, ANCA, antiphospholipid antibodies, complement) returned negative, arguing against these etiologies | "The rheumatology workup ... were unremarkable."
3. Primary viral myocarditis explored, prompting broad PCR testing of myocardium for enteroviruses, herpesviruses, influenza, etc.; all assays were negative, ruling out active viral infection | "Nested (RT‑) PCR for the detection of ... was negative in the myocardium and EDTA blood."
4. Active SARS‑CoV‑2 infection evaluated by qRT‑PCR on myocardial tissue, which was negative, excluding direct viral myocardial invasion | "In addition, qRT‑PCR did not detect SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA in the myocardium."
5. Prior SARS‑CoV‑2 exposure evidenced by positive anti‑S1 and anti‑N antibodies, supporting a post‑infectious process rather than acute infection | "Microbiological investigation only revealed positive SARS‑CoV‑2 serology (anti‑S1 and anti‑N antibodies)."
6. Multisystem involvement (cardiac failure, rash, gastrointestinal edema, renal and hepatic dysfunction) together with marked hyperinflammation (elevated IL‑6, CRP) aligned with the diagnostic criteria for MIS‑C | (implicit from cumulative clinical picture described in the case).

case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with a 5‑day history of progressively worsening left‑temporal headache accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He had received the first dose of the ChAdOx1 nCoV‑19 (Oxford‑AstraZeneca) vaccine 10 days prior. Past medical history was notable for lymphoma treated with autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation 9 years earlier, hyperlipidemia, and chronic hepatitis B carriage. Family history included systemic lupus erythematosus in his mother, two sisters and daughter, and rheumatoid arthritis in his brother. On examination his blood pressure was 129/90 mm Hg, temperature 35.4 °C, heart rate 67 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 96 % on room air. He rated his headache 9/10 on a numerical rating scale. He denied visual changes, seizures, focal weakness, dyspnea, or abdominal pain; there were no petechiae and neurologic exam was non‑focal.

Initial laboratory studies showed a D‑dimer >20 mg/L and thrombocytopenia (platelet count 99 000/µL, prior baseline 182 000/µL). Nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 nucleic acid amplification was negative. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated dural sinus thrombosis involving the left transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and left distal internal jugular vein. Chest computed tomography revealed filling defects in the left upper lobe consistent with pulmonary embolism. Abdominal CT showed no visceral thrombosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recent adenoviral vector COVID‑19 vaccination coupled with thrombosis at unusual sites and thrombocytopenia raised suspicion for VITT. | "He had received the first dose of the ChAdOx1 nCoV‑19 (Oxford‑AstraZeneca) vaccine 10 days prior to his admission... elevated D‑dimer level... thrombocytopenia... dural sinus thrombosis..."
2. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) was considered but excluded by normal ADAMTS13 activity (87.2 %) and absence of schistocytes. | "ADAMTS13, 87.2% (40‑130%); decreased platelet count from a peripheral blood smear without schistocytes."
3. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) was excluded by normal hemoglobin, haptoglobin, LDH, and lack of hemolysis. | "hemoglobin 13.3 g/dL; haptoglobin 132.4 mg/dL; lactate dehydrogenase 153 U/L; no schistocytes."
4. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and antiphospholipid syndrome were ruled out by negative ANA, anti‑dsDNA, anti‑cardiolipin, anti‑β2‑glycoprotein 1, and normal complement levels. | "negative ANA titer; anti‑dsDNA <0.5 IU/mL; lupus anticoagulant 0.96 (<1.20); anti‑cardiolipin IgG <0.5 IU/mL; anti‑beta2 glycoprotein 1 <0.6 U/mL."
5. Rheumatoid arthritis was excluded by negative rheumatoid factor and lack of clinical signs. | "rheumatoid factor <10 IU/mL (<14.0 IU/mL)."
6. Inherited thrombophilias (protein C, protein S, antithrombin III deficiencies) were ruled out by normal activity levels. | "protein C, 100.1% (70‑140%); protein S, 85.2% (72.2‑126%); antithrombin III, 91.9% (75‑125%)."
7. Hyperhomocysteinemia was excluded by normal homocysteine concentration. | "homocysteine, 10.10 µmol/L (5.0‑15.0 µmol/L)."
8. Underlying hematologic malignancy was deemed unlikely given stable lymphoma follow‑up and absence of new cytopenias or blasts. | "regular follow‑up at the outpatient department; no evidence of hematologic malignancies."
9. A strongly positive anti‑PF4 antibody (>200 OD, reference 3.055) in the absence of heparin exposure confirmed VITT. | "a confirmatory test for anti‑PF4 antibody later showed >200 (reference optical density value 3.055), without previous exposure to heparin."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has several diseases listed in the 21 SELECTED list (covid_19, cryptococcosis, tuberculosis). The case provides sufficient laboratory and imaging evidence to unequivocally diagnose **tuberculosis** (positive urine LAM, miliary pattern on chest X‑ray, GeneXpert positive). This will be the primary target diagnosis for the teaching case.  
2. Breakpoint: Include all presenting data up to and including the urine LAM result, chest radiograph description, and GeneXpert result, as well as CD 4 count and relevant negative studies. Stop **before** the authors explicitly state the composite diagnosis (“A diagnosis of severe COVID‑19 … with complications of CM, disseminated tuberculosis…”). This gives students enough clues to deduce disseminated tuberculosis while avoiding spoilers.  
3. Analytic Distinctions (as presented by the authors):  
   • COVID‑19 infection confirmed by RT‑PCR and antigen test, but pulmonary findings (miliary nodules) are atypical for primary COVID‑19 pneumonia, prompting search for additional opportunistic infection.  
   • Cryptococcal meningitis supported by positive serum and CSF CrAg; explains meningeal signs but does not account for the miliary pattern on chest imaging.  
   • Disseminated tuberculosis supported by three independent tests (urine LAM, chest X‑ray miliary pattern, GeneXpert positive) and the patient’s profound immunosuppression (CD4 = 32 cells/µL).  
   • Other potential infections (malaria, bacterial sepsis) were investigated and excluded by negative blood smear and negative bacterial cultures.
case_prompt:
A 37‑year‑old nulliparous woman with a recent diagnosis of HIV infection (not on antiretroviral therapy) was admitted to the Mulago National Referral Hospital COVID‑19 Treatment Unit with a 3‑day history of worsening cough and dyspnea. She had a productive cough with mucoid sputum, evening fevers, and a 2‑month history of weight loss. Over the prior 5 days she experienced anosmia, high‑grade intermittent fevers, headaches, altered mentation, an episode of loss of consciousness, and myalgias. Four days before referral, a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by RT‑PCR and rapid antigen testing. She tested HIV‑positive 8 days earlier and was not receiving antiretrovirals or cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.

On presentation she was critically ill: axillary temperature 38.5 °C, heart rate 168 bpm, respiratory rate 32 /min, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, random glucose 8.7 mmol/L, oxygen saturation 85‑90 % on 5 L /min nasal prongs. Exam showed nasal flaring, intercostal recessions, bilateral coarse crepitations, Glasgow coma scale 8/15, neck stiffness with a positive Kernig’s sign. Laboratory studies revealed: positive serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen, negative blood smear for Plasmodium, WBC 11.8 × 10³/µL (neutrophils 91.6 %, lymphocytes 4.5 %), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL with MCV 67 fL, platelets 300 × 10³/µL, normal renal and liver panels, blood group B Rh D positive, urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) positive (Grade II), chest radiograph showing miliary nodules with ground‑glass opacities, and unenhanced brain CT demonstrating a large right‑sided hypodense territory consistent with middle cerebral artery infarction. GeneXpert testing of sputum was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis without rifampicin resistance. CD4⁺ count was 32 cells/µL; HIV viral load was not available. Urine β‑hCG was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 pneumonia considered due to recent positive RT‑PCR and respiratory symptoms | "Four days prior to referral … nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 was positive on both reverse transcriptase‑polymerase chain reaction (RT‑PCR) and rapid antigen tests."
2. Bacterial community‑acquired pneumonia considered because of productive cough and crepitations, but excluded by negative aerobic/anaerobic cultures and lack of focal lobar consolidation | "Anaerobic, aerobic, fungal and mycobacterial cultures were negative."
3. Cryptococcal meningitis considered given meningismus and altered mentation; confirmed by positive serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen but does not explain miliary pulmonary pattern | "Her serum and cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) tests were positive."
4. Malaria considered as a febrile illness in Uganda; excluded by negative blood smear | "A blood smear was negative for Plasmodium and other haemoparasites."
5. Disseminated tuberculosis is the unifying diagnosis for pulmonary (miliary pattern), urinary (positive LAM), and molecular (GeneXpert positive) findings in an immunocompromised host | "The urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) was positive (Grade II)." – "Chest radiography revealed features of miliary tuberculosis with background ground glass opacities." – "The GeneXpert was positive without rifampicin resistance."
6. Anemia considered as a contributing factor but identified as microcytic and likely secondary to chronic disease or iron deficiency rather than primary cause of acute respiratory failure | "She had a microcytic anemia with hemoglobin level of 8.5 g/dL and mean corpuscular volume of 67 fL."

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors excluded common causes of headache (e.g., tension‑type, migraine), cardiac ischemia, hypercoagulable disorders (antiphospholipid antibodies, Factor V Leiden), neoplastic recurrence, and intracranial hemorrhage/mass through normal labs, imaging, and echocardiography, finally attributing the findings to cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old man with a past medical history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, hypothyroidism, and head‑and‑neck cancer treated 11 years ago presented for evaluation of headaches. He reported waking from sleep with a pounding headache two to three times per month over the past 6 months, accompanied by palpitations, dizziness, and diaphoresis. He denied blurred vision, speech changes, focal neurologic deficits, nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, cough, nasal congestion, fatigue, or diarrhea. Ibuprofen 200 mg (two to three tablets) relieved the pain. Outpatient MRI brain was performed and revealed findings suspicious for cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; he was referred to the emergency department.

Three months earlier he tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 after a workplace exposure, with cough, headache, and nasal congestion that resolved with basic care. On admission he again tested positive for COVID‑19. He denied smoking, alcohol, or recreational drug use. Vital signs were within normal limits; oxygen saturation was normal on room air. Physical examination, including a complete neurologic exam, was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, potassium 5.2 mmol/L, normal TSH. Antiphospholipid antibody panel was negative except for a mildly positive IgM cardiolipin (21 GPL). Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations were negative. Telemetry demonstrated bigeminy and trigeminy without chest discomfort or ischemic changes; a two‑dimensional echocardiogram was normal. Non‑contrast CT brain showed no acute hemorrhage, mass effect, or evidence of tumor recurrence, only chronic small‑vessel ischemic changes. MRI brain demonstrated an abnormal FLAIR signal with loss of flow void in the distal left transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and jugular bulb.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Common primary headache disorders considered but unlikely given nocturnal onset, autonomic symptoms, and refractory nature. | "He reported waking from sleep with a pounding headache…associated with palpitations, dizziness, and diaphoresis."
2. Cardiac ischemia or arrhythmia as cause of chest discomfort excluded by absence of symptoms and normal echo. | "He had no complaints of chest discomfort; there were no signs of ischemia, and a subsequent two‑dimensional echo was within normal limits."
3. Antiphospholipid syndrome evaluated; negative beta‑2‑glycoprotein antibodies and mostly negative cardiolipin antibodies made it unlikely. | "IgG, IgM, and IgA beta‑2 glycoprotein antibodies were all within normal limits. IgG, IgA cardiolipin antibodies were within normal limits, but IgM was mildly positive at 21."
4. Inherited thrombophilia (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation) ruled out by negative genetic testing. | "Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations were negative."
5. Neoplastic recurrence excluded by imaging showing no new mass or tumor. | "There was no evidence of recurrence of his known cancer."
6. Intracranial hemorrhage or mass lesion ruled out by non‑contrast CT (no acute bleed, mass effect) and MRI (no enhancing mass). | "CT brain imaging without contrast revealed no acute intracranial hemorrhage, midline shift, or mass effect…MRI brain findings showed an abnormal FLAIR signal…" (no mention of mass).
7. COVID‑19 infection present but mild; considered as a possible pro‑thrombotic trigger but not sufficient alone to explain imaging findings. | "He again tested for COVID‑19 and tested positive…His symptoms improved with basic medical management."
8. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis best fits the combination of headache pattern, MRI loss of flow void in the left transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and jugular bulb, and absence of alternative explanations. | "MRI brain findings showed an abnormal FLAIR signal with loss of flow void in the distal left transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, and jugular bulb."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: Identification: The patient ultimately met criteria for catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE. A concurrent SARS‑CoV‑2 infection (covid_19) is present, but CAPS is the primary focus of the report.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the case presentation after the chest CT that demonstrated a left adrenal mass concerning for adrenal hemorrhage, and after the repeat laboratory panel showing falling hemoglobin and platelet count, but before the authors present the direct antiglobulin test, hemolysis work‑up, new neurologic deficits, and the explicit statement that the patient “met the criteria for CAPS.”
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished CAPS from isolated COVID‑19 coagulopathy, heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia, and disseminated intravascular coagulation by highlighting (a) simultaneous arterial and venous thromboses, (b) multiorgan involvement (adrenal hemorrhage, retroperitoneal bleed, watershed infarcts), (c) catastrophic rise in antiphospholipid antibody titers, and (d) laboratory evidence of immune‑mediated hemolysis and severe coagulopathy despite therapeutic anticoagulation.
case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and triple‑positive antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) presented with acute encephalopathy. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination was notable only for altered mental status. Initial labs showed hemoglobin 131 g/L, white‑blood‑cell count 11.8 × 10⁹/L, absolute lymphocyte count 1.5 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 173 × 10⁹/L, and D‑dimer 0.54 µg/mL. Brain MRI demonstrated chronic microvascular ischemia. Therapeutic unfractionated heparin was started because of her APS history and prior venous thrombotic events.

On hospital day 10 she developed fever and hypoxia and tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2. Dexamethasone and remdesivir were initiated; remdesivir was stopped after three days due to worsening renal function. Subsequent labs revealed hemoglobin 86 g/L, white‑blood‑cell count 11 × 10⁹/L, absolute lymphocyte count 0.77 × 10⁹/L, and platelet count 93 × 10⁹/L. Antiphospholipid antibody testing remained strongly positive (lupus anticoagulant positive; cardiolipin IgG > 112 U/mL, IgA > 65 U/mL; β2‑glycoprotein I IgG > 112 U/mL, IgA > 65 U/mL). Platelets fell further to 67 × 10⁹/L. Coagulation studies showed prothrombin time 23.3 s, INR 2.1, activated partial thromboplastin time 132 s, fibrinogen 832 mg/dL, and D‑dimer 1.56 µg/mL.

The following day she required non‑invasive ventilation for acute respiratory distress. Chest CT revealed diffuse bilateral ground‑glass opacities and a 4.3‑cm left adrenal mass concerning for adrenal hemorrhage. Intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg was started. By hospital day 19 her hemoglobin had fallen markedly and imaging demonstrated a retroperitoneal hemorrhage. Anticoagulation was held, and she later developed an acute right‑sided superficial femoral vein thrombosis; an inferior vena cava filter was placed because of anticoagulation intolerance.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent and worsening thrombocytopenia with prolonged PT/PTT and markedly elevated D‑dimer suggested a consumptive coagulopathy but not classic DIC, as fibrinogen remained high (832 mg/dL) and there was ongoing arterial thrombosis. | "prothrombin time of 23.3 seconds, international normalized ratio of 2.1, activated partial thromboplastin time of 132 seconds, fibrinogen activity of 832 mg/dL, and D‑dimer of 1.56 µg/mL."
2. The recent exposure to heparin raised the possibility of heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia, yet the platelet drop occurred in the context of rising antiphospholipid antibodies and multiorgan thromboses, making HIT less likely. | "Therapeutic unfractionated heparin was initiated... platelet count had decreased to 67 × 10⁹/L."
3. Severe COVID‑19 infection can cause coagulopathy and adrenal involvement, but the presence of a left adrenal mass consistent with hemorrhage, new retroperitoneal bleed, and a surge in antiphospholipid antibody titers pointed toward APS‑related catastrophic events rather than isolated viral‑mediated injury. | "CT of the chest demonstrated ... a 4.3 cm left adrenal mass, concerning in terms of adrenal hemorrhage."
4. The combination of new arterial (brain watershed infarctions) and venous (superficial femoral vein) thromboses, adrenal hemorrhage, and rapid deterioration despite anticoagulation fulfilled the clinical criteria for catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome. | "With new‑onset ischemic stroke, acute venous thrombosis, and adrenal hemorrhage, the patient met the criteria for CAPS."
5. Laboratory evidence of immune‑mediated hemolysis (positive direct antiglobulin test, low haptoglobin, high LDH) supported an underlying autoimmune process consistent with CAPS and helped exclude isolated sepsis‑related anemia. | "A direct antiglobulin test was positive, serum haptoglobin concentration was low, and serum lactate dehydrogenase concentration was elevated."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient ultimately had a splenic infarction, which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. COVID-19 (covid_19) is present but was already confirmed on admission and is not the mystery to be solved. Therefore, the target diagnosis for the teaching case is an OUT_OF_SCOPE disease: splenic infarction.
2. Breakpoint: Present the case up to the onset of abdominal symptoms and physical findings, stopping before the CT‑scan result that confirms splenic infarction. This supplies enough clinical clues (abdominal pain, thrombocytosis, normal abdominal exam) for the learner to generate a differential and anticipate an intra‑abdominal thrombotic event without revealing the diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors established the splenic infarction by (a) noting new abdominal pain and laboratory evidence of thrombocytosis, (b) performing contrast CT that demonstrated splenic artery thrombosis and a 75 % infarct, and (c) emphasizing that prior imaging was negative, indicating an acute event despite therapeutic anticoagulation. Competing possibilities (e.g., other sources of abdominal pain, other thrombotic complications) were implicitly excluded by the normal abdominal exam and lack of other embolic lesions on imaging.
case_prompt:
A 31‑year‑old Caucasian woman, 26 weeks pregnant, BMI 29, with no prior medical history, was admitted with 5 days of progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and dry cough. Real‑time PCR was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 and chest CT demonstrated COVID‑19 pneumonia involving 90 % of the lungs. Five days after admission she required ICU transfer for severe dyspnea, polypnea, and extreme hypoxemia; she was promptly intubated and placed on controlled mechanical ventilation with continuous neuromuscular blockade. The PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio was 78, and lung compliance was low. Her respiratory course was complicated by two tension pneumothoraces that were drained and by ventilator‑associated pneumonia treated according to culture results. After treatment, pulmonary status improved and she met extubation criteria 16 days after the initial intubation. Cardiac function remained normal; vasopressor support was needed during septic episodes to keep MAP > 70 mm Hg. Renal function stayed normal. Post‑extubation she exhibited normal cognition but severe neuropathy and myopathy.

Therapies included a 10‑day Remdesivir course started on day 5, dexamethasone from admission, therapeutic enoxaparin (1 mg/kg bid) plus aspirin, and a single dose of tocilizumab after an IL‑6 rise on day 5. Lopinavir/ritonavir was begun at admission. Daily obstetric ultrasound showed a viable fetus with progressively decreasing umbilical cord blood flow; ten days after admission intra‑uterine fetal demise was diagnosed and a cesarean section performed.

During hospitalization she reported mild, dull abdominal pain and developed progressive thrombocytosis. Physical examination revealed a soft, non‑distended, non‑tender abdomen.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tension pneumothorax considered as cause of acute respiratory worsening but excluded for abdominal pain because it is a thoracic event; "two episodes of tension pneumothorax, adequately drained" – no abdominal findings related.  
2. Ventilator‑associated pneumonia accounted for febrile and septic episodes but did not explain new abdominal pain; "ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP) treated according to cultures" – no abdominal involvement.  
3. Septic shock and vasopressor use could cause abdominal ischemia, yet prior CT and physical exam were normal; "both the therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH and the antiplatelet therapy were continued after the diagnosis of the thrombotic event" – indicating no other organ infarction before.  
4. Pregnancy‑related complications (e.g., placental insufficiency, HELLP syndrome) were considered given abnormal umbilical flow, but the abdomen remained soft, non‑distended, and non‑tender; "clinical examination showed a soft, non‑distended, non‑tender abdomen."  
5. Acute splenic infarction confirmed by imaging after the onset of abdominal pain; "CT‑scan confirmed a 75 % splenic infarction, with splenic artery thrombosis, with a major reduction in blood flow." This finding, together with new thrombocytosis, established the diagnosis.

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient is ultimately diagnosed with HIV infection (AIDS), which is on the SELECTED diseases list as “hiv_aids”.
2. Best breakpoint: Include all presenting information up to the point where clinicians decide to test for HIV, but stop before the ELISA result is disclosed. This gives sufficient history, exam, and initial laboratory data for the learner to consider HIV as the most plausible diagnosis without revealing the confirmatory test.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished HIV/AIDS from other dermatologic and infectious etiologies by (a) noting lack of response to antifungals, steroids, and dapsone; (b) documenting negative serologies for syphilis, hepatitis B/C, HSV; (c) ruling out TB exposure; (d) observing atypical ophthalmic findings; and (e) finally confirming HIV seropositivity with ELISA and low CD4 count.
case_prompt:
A 45‑year‑old Bangladeshi woman presented in May 2020 with severe generalized itching and skin lesions involving the extremities, neck, upper back, chest, oral cavity, and genitalia for the past four years. She now reported a gradual loss of vision in both eyes over one month, accompanied by recurrent fever and weight loss for the same duration. Her husband, residing in South Africa for eight years, suffers from a similar skin lesion; other family members are well. She denied any history of tuberculosis or contact with smear‑positive tuberculosis patients and had never received a blood transfusion.

On examination she appeared emaciated, moderately anemic, with normal vital signs and no lymphadenopathy. Skin survey revealed multiple excoriated, lichenified papules with exudation and crusting over the extremities, neck, and upper back, along with whitish patches on the tongue and oral cavity and a non‑healing ulcer on the labia. Syphilis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HSV infections were evaluated because of the mucocutaneous lesions; all serologies were negative, making these unlikely | "Other investigations including the serum venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test, TPHA, serum hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), antibody against HCV, and antibodies (IgM + IgG) against HSV 1 and 2 were negative."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient presents with a progressive fatigue syndrome, brain fog, concentration difficulties, and imbalances after two mild COVID‑19 infections, fulfilling standardized CFS criteria. Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list, while COVID‑19 is; however COVID‑19 is a prior infection, not the mystery diagnosis. Hence the target is an OUT_OF_SCOPE disease → chronic fatigue syndrome.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the presentation just before the description of the BC 007 infusion and its outcomes. Include the history of COVID‑19 infections, onset of fatigue, neurological symptoms, standardized fatigue scores, blood pressure elevation, and the pre‑existing auto‑antibody profile, but stop before “After and during the infusion of BC 007…”.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors link persistent auto‑antibodies (ss2‑AAb, AT‑1‑AAb, α1‑AAb, MAS‑AAb, M2‑AAb) to impaired retinal microcirculation and chronic fatigue. They argue that conventional ocular or vascular disease cannot explain the systemic fatigue, thereby justifying therapeutic targeting of the auto‑antibodies with BC 007.
case_prompt: A 59‑year‑old man with a 17‑year history of glaucoma presented with a two‑year course of fatigue‑related complaints. He experienced two mild COVID‑19 infections, the first in April 2020 (no hospitalization) and a presumed second infection around the turn of the year, after which he noted worsening loss of taste and a progressive fatigue syndrome beginning in January 2021. Two months later he developed neurological symptoms described as brain fog, lack of concentration, and balance disturbances. In May 2021 his fatigue was quantified using the Canadian Consensus Criteria (score 11), the Chalder Fatigue Scale (score 27), and the Bell Score (70), indicating severe limitation of daily activities. An elevated diastolic blood pressure was also noted. He has been enrolled in the Erlanger Glaucoma Registry, with pre‑existing seropositivity for ss2‑AAb for 12 years. After the first COVID‑19 infection his auto‑antibody profile persisted and additional auto‑antibodies targeting the angiotensin‑1 receptor (AT‑1‑AAb), α1‑adrenergic receptor (α1‑AAb), MAS receptor (MAS‑AAb), and muscarinic‑2 receptor (M2‑AAb) were detected using a cardiomyocyte bioassay. Ophthalmic examination showed best‑corrected visual acuity of 0.8 (right eye) and 0.6 (left eye), intraocular pressures of 13 mm Hg bilaterally under tafluprost, and prior Nd:YAG iridotomy, trabeculectomy, and cataract surgery on the left eye. Optical coherence tomography‑angiography revealed impaired capillary microcirculation in the macula and peripapillary region compared with normative data. No SARS‑CoV‑2 vaccination had been administered before the planned intervention. Given the auto‑antibody profile and its presumed link to retinal microvascular impairment and chronic fatigue, the team decided to attempt treatment with the aptamer BC 007, aiming to (1) eliminate GPCR‑targeting auto‑antibodies and (2) improve retinal microcirculation, with the additional goal of alleviating chronic fatigue syndrome.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Chronic fatigue syndrome (post‑COVID) is supported by the temporal relationship to mild COVID‑19 infections, progressive fatigue, brain fog, concentration deficits, balance problems, and markedly abnormal fatigue scores (Canadian Criteria 11, Chalder 27, Bell 70) | "progressive fatigue syndrome starting on January 2021... brain fog, lack of concentration, and imbalances."
2. Depressive or primary psychiatric disorder was considered less likely because the patient met specific objective CFS criteria and no mood symptoms were described; the authors focused on auto‑antibody–mediated mechanisms rather than mood disorder | "We intended to improve chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS)."
3. Glaucoma‑related ocular vascular impairment was excluded as a cause of systemic fatigue, given that the ophthalmic findings (optic disc cupping, reduced visual acuity, prior surgeries) are localized and do not explain the generalized neuro‑cognitive symptoms | "Optic disc displayed glaucomatous alterations... impaired capillary microcirculation in the macula and peripapillary region compared to normative data."
4. Hypertension alone was deemed insufficient to account for the constellation of fatigue and neurocognitive deficits; blood pressure elevation was noted but not presented as the primary diagnosis | "diastolic blood pressure was increased."
5. Ongoing COVID‑19 infection was ruled out because both infections were mild, resolved without hospitalization, and no acute viral symptoms were present at the time of presentation | "No severe symptoms were monitored during both COVID‑19 infections regarding the necessity of hospitalization."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately diagnoses acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) associated with prior SARS‑CoV‑2 infection. AIN is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list; covid_19 is on the list but was already known before the diagnostic work‑up. Therefore the mystery to be solved by the presented data is AIN, an OUT_OF_SCOPE disease.  
2. Best Breakpoint: Include all presenting symptoms, vital signs, physical exam, initial laboratory results, serology confirming prior SARS‑CoV‑2 infection, renal ultrasound findings, and the statement that “AIN was suspected and the patient underwent a kidney biopsy,” but stop before any biopsy pathology results (IHC, EM) and before the therapeutic response is described. This provides enough information for learners to formulate a differential for acute kidney injury and consider AIN without revealing the definitive pathology.  
3. Key Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished AIN from other AKI etiologies by (a) the temporal relationship to a recent mild COVID‑19 infection, (b) absence of nephrotoxic drug exposure, (c) laboratory pattern of glucosuria, low‑molecular‑weight proteinuria, microhematuria, and leukocyturia with casts, (d) normal complement, negative EBV/CMV serology, negative ANA and normal calcium, and (e) renal ultrasound showing diffuse parenchymal changes rather than obstruction. case_prompt:
The patient was referred to our tertiary care center due to general malaise, loss of appetite, increased thirst, and a significant increase in serum creatinine. The patient was an otherwise healthy 12‑year‑old boy who had a RT‑PCR confirmed SARS‑CoV‑2 infection with mild respiratory symptoms 7 weeks before the admission. The aforementioned clinical symptoms started ~1 week after the infection. The patient had no history of non‑steroid anti‑inflammatory drugs or other medication use prior to the development of symptoms or admission to the hospital. On admission, the patient was afebrile, had normal blood pressure and clinical examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Blood tests revealed severe impairment of kidney function (serum creatinine 235 µmol/L), high erythrocyte‑sedimentation rate, anemia, thrombocytosis, and increased C‑reactive protein. Urine tests showed glucosuria, low‑molecular‑weight proteinuria, and microhematuria, mild leukocyturia with hyaline and granular casts on microscopy. Antibodies against SARS‑CoV‑2 S protein receptor‑binding domain confirmed prior infection with high titers (453 BAU/mL). Kidney ultrasound showed bilateral parenchymal thickening and hyperechogenicity with normal corticomedullary differentiation. AIN was suspected and the patient underwent a kidney biopsy.

The complement levels of the patient were normal and no evidence of recent Epstein‑Barr (EBV) or cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections was found by serologic testing. Additional workup that included ophthalmological evaluation for uveitis, anti‑nuclear antibodies, and total serum calcium levels were all normal.

Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors first pursued common pandemic‑related respira­tory infections (COVID‑19, bacterial CAP) and thrombo‑embolic disease, then shifted focus when imaging revealed a cystic liver lesion with characteristic features (membrane, wall breach, biliary communication) that favored a parasitic etiology over simple cyst, abscess, or neoplasm.
case_prompt:
A male patient of North African origin in his late twenties was brought to the emergency department after four days of abdominal pain, fever, diarrhea, and dyspnea. He had no notable medical history. On arrival his vital signs were: temperature 38.2 °C, heart rate 128 beats/min, respiratory rate 40 breaths/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 87 % on room air. Physical exam showed mild right‑upper‑quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs.

Laboratory studies revealed an elevated D‑dimer of 3344 ng/dL, C‑reactive protein 15 mg/L, and alkaline phosphatase 136.8 U/L. Chest radiography demonstrated a right lower‑lobe opacity, and arterial blood gas showed a PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio of 150, indicating hypoxaemia. A nasopharyngeal RT‑PCR test for SARS‑CoV‑2 was negative.

Given the concern for severe community‑acquired pneumonia, intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin were started, and hydroxychloroquine plus lopinavir/ritonavir were added for possible non‑bacterial infection. Because of worsening respiratory distress and hypotension, enoxaparin infusion was initiated and a CT pulmonary angiogram was performed to exclude pulmonary embolism. The CTA showed segmental atelectasis in the right lower lobe without overt pulmonary infection, but incidentally noted a cystic lesion in the liver on the upper abdominal sections.

An abdominal CT scan was then obtained, which demonstrated a cyst in hepatic segments V/V​I containing a detached hyperdense membrane floating within the cyst cavity. In a posterior subcapsular region a wall defect was identified, associated with focal intra‑hepatic bile duct dilatation extending to the cyst. Adjacent fat stranding and a small volume of free perihepatic fluid were also present.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe pneumonia was considered based on fever, dyspnea, right‑lower‑lobe opacity, and hypoxaemia | "Based on the initial workup, a severe pneumonia was suspected..."
2. COVID‑19 infection remained a concern despite a negative test because of the pandemic context | "...the majority of ED visits at that moment of the pandemic was still due to this virus."
3. Pulmonary embolism was investigated given tachycardia, hypotension, and hypoxaemia | "CT pulmonary angiogram was requested to rule out pulmonary embolism (PE)."
4. Simple hepatic cyst or abscess were possible explanations for the incidentally found cystic liver lesion | (implicit from imaging description; the authors did not name these but the lack of enhancing wall or purulent material suggested otherwise)
5. Intrabiliary rupture or direct cyst rupture leading to anaphylaxis were entertained based on cyst wall defect, biliary dilatation, fat stranding, and free fluid | "In a posterior subcapsular region a wall defect was observed, associated to a focal intrahepatic bile duct dilatation... Fat stranding and a small amount of free perihepatic fluid were also present."
6. The combination of a detached hyperdense membrane within the cyst and a wall defect strongly points toward a parasitic hydatid (echinococcal) cyst rather than other cystic liver lesions | "detached hyperdense membrane floating within the cyst."

case_prompt:
At 5 years of age, the patient was admitted with a 3‑week history of cutaneous changes affecting her face and upper limbs but was otherwise well. Her grandfather, who co‑habited with the family, had developed a febrile illness and tested positive for COVID‑19 by PCR a few weeks previously. Despite this, she had no history of fever, cough, or other systemic symptoms. No other family member was unwell, including the patient’s sibling, who remained well and completely asymptomatic.  

On physical examination of the new skin changes, there were dusky areas of induration involving the central and lower face, bilateral forearms, and extending onto her hands with associated oedema. There was notable sparing of dependent areas, including the back and posterior legs. Scattered petechial macules were also noted on the left forearm and foot. Aside from the cutaneous changes, no other extraneurological signs were found on examination. She was afebrile and the remaining observations were within the normal range.  

Investigations demonstrated a mild transaminitis with an ALT of 49 U/L (9–25), a raised amylase of 153 U/L (25–101), D‑dimer of 1,785 µg/L (<500), and lactate dehydrogenase of 525 U/L (192–321). Throat swabs for SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA PCR were negative. Of note, chest radiography, renal function, autoimmune studies, and C‑reactive protein levels were normal; however, there was a significant elevation in the terminal complement complex (TCC) at this stage at 244 ng/mL (0–80).

1. Consideration of SARS‑CoV‑2 infection despite negative PCR because of recent household exposure and complement activation | "Her grandfather… tested positive for COVID‑19… Throat swabs for SARS‑CoV‑2 RNA PCR were negative… there was a significant elevation in the terminal complement complex (TCC) at this stage at 244 ng/ml (0‑80)."
2. Bacterial sepsis deemed unlikely given afebrile state, normal CRP, and lack of systemic signs | "She was afebrile and the remaining observations were within the normal range… C‑reactive protein levels were normal."
3. Classic Kawasaki disease deemed unlikely because of absence of fever, conjunctivitis, mucosal changes, and normal inflammatory markers | "No other extraneurological signs were found on examination… C‑reactive protein levels were normal."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s primary clinical problem is a delayed, unreduced fracture‑dislocation of the right elbow. The only disease from the 21‑disease list mentioned is COVID‑19, which is part of the past medical history and not the focus of diagnostic work‑up. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best breakpoint: Include presentation, history of trauma, COVID‑19 infection, physical‑examination findings, and the initial radiographic/CT imaging that demonstrate anterior elbow dislocation with medial epicondyle and comminuted lateral condyle fractures. Stop before the description of the surgical plan (“We planned an open reduction internal fixation…”) so the learner has all data needed to deduce the fracture‑dislocation without being given the treatment details.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out infection (no signs, no cultures), ruled out neurovascular compromise (intact exam), and used plain radiographs and CT with 3‑D reconstruction to confirm the exact pattern of dislocation and fractures, thereby establishing the need for operative fixation.
case_prompt:
A 30‑year‑old man presented to the outpatient department with pain, deformity of the right elbow and a non‑healing wound persisting for 5 weeks. He reported a road‑traffic accident while riding a two‑wheeler, after which he sustained pain, swelling and deformity of the right elbow with a wound over the olecranon. He was initially treated at a local hospital, tested positive for COVID‑19 and managed conservatively with a posterior above‑elbow slab. After recovery from COVID‑19 he returned because the deformity and stiffness persisted.

On examination the right elbow showed a flexion deformity, wasting of the arm and forearm muscles, and an anteriorly displaced olecranon process. A 3 × 2 cm non‑healing wound was present over the olecranon. There were no signs of active infection and no neurovascular deficit. Flexion was limited to 30° (further flexion possible to 60°); pronation was 10° and supination up to 40°. Valgus laxity was noted.

Radiographs demonstrated an anterior dislocation of the right elbow with a medial epicondyle fracture and a comminuted lateral condyle fracture. Computed tomography with three‑dimensional reconstruction confirmed an anterior elbow dislocation associated with a multi‑fragmentary lateral condyle fracture and a medial epicondyle fracture (AO/OTA Classification 13‑B1.3).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infection considered but excluded because “There were no signs of active infection, and therefore, blood culture was not done.”  
2. Neurovascular injury considered but excluded as “no associated neurovascular deficit” was documented on exam.  
3. Simple elbow dislocation without fracture considered less likely after imaging showed “anteriorly dislocated … with medial epicondyle fracture and comminuted lateral condyle fracture,” confirming a fracture‑dislocation.  
4. Chronic post‑COVID musculoskeletal sequelae considered but the pattern of trauma‑related bony injury on CT (multifragmentary fractures) pointed toward a traumatic fracture‑dislocation rather than a post‑viral arthropathy. “Computed tomography … confirmed an anterior dislocation … and the associated distal humerus … fracture.”

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s pivotal unresolved diagnosis is rhino‑orbital‑cerebral mucormycosis, which is **not** on the 21 SELECTED diseases list; therefore it is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to **Day 3 of admission**, i.e., after development of right‑eye swelling and addition of vancomycin for presumed orbital cellulitis, but **before** the explicit consideration of rhino‑orbital mucormycosis on Day 4. This provides the clinical clues (COVID‑19, steroid use, uncontrolled hyperglycaemia, orbital signs) necessary for students to work toward the diagnosis without revealing it.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished mucormycosis from bacterial pneumonia, orbital cellulitis, and diabetic ketoacidosis by (a) noting necrotic facial tissue requiring debridement, (b) lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and (c) rapid progression despite glycaemic control, prompting antifungal therapy and imaging suggestive of invasive fungal disease.
case_prompt:
A 39‑year‑old woman with lifelong cerebral palsy presented in July 2021 to a COVID‑19 treatment center with worsening shortness of breath, easy fatigability, low‑grade fever, chills, frontal headache, and a ten‑day history of productive cough with yellowish sputum. She had tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by RT‑PCR five days earlier. Her chronic medications included sodium valproate 200 mg PO daily; two weeks prior she had been diagnosed with acute angle‑closure glaucoma of the right eye and was using timolol 0.5 % eye drops BID, tropicamide 1 % TID, acetazolamide 250 mg PO BID, and prednisolone 20 mg PO daily.

She was transferred from a local health centre after receiving dexamethasone, azithromycin, and ceftriaxone‑sulbactam. In the emergency department her vitals were BP 120/80 mmHg, pulse 92/min, RR 32/min, temperature 36.2 °C, and SpO₂ 96 % on 6 L/min facemask oxygen. Examination revealed coarse crepitations over the left lung. Random blood glucose was >600 mg/dL; urine showed +1 ketones and +3 glucosuria. Chest X‑ray showed left‑sided pneumonia. Initial labs demonstrated mild leukocytosis (14.4 × 10³ WBC/µL with 95 % neutrophils, 0.9 % lymphocytes), moderate hyponatremia (127 mmol/L), mild hypokalemia (3.2 mmol/L), pre‑renal azotemia (creatinine 2.95 mg/dL, BUN 69 mg/dL), CRP 89.9 mg/L, and HIV serology was negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal kidneys. Arterial blood gas was not obtained.

She was admitted to the ICU with a problem list of severe COVID‑19 with superimposed bacterial pneumonia, pre‑renal AKI, stress‑induced hyperglycaemia (possible ketosis‑prone type 2 diabetes), cerebral palsy, and right‑eye glaucoma. Treatment included dexamethasone 6 mg IV daily, ceftriaxone‑sulbactam 1.5 g IV BID, unfractionated heparin, vitamin C, zinc, and a DKA protocol. 

On hospital day 2, right‑eye swelling developed and orbital cellulitis was added; renal‑dose‑adjusted vancomycin was started. On day 3, NPH insulin 16/8 U SC BID with correctional regular insulin was initiated due to persistent hyperglycaemia. By the end of day 3, insulin requirements were being titrated upward.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Severe COVID‑19 with bacterial superinfection was initially suspected because of a positive RT‑PCR, left‑sided pneumonia on chest X‑ray, and leukocytosis. | "problem list of severe COVID-19 with superimposed bacterial pneumonia"  
2. Diabetic ketoacidosis was considered given hyperglycaemia >600 mg/dL, ketonuria, and glucosuria; it was treated per protocol but later deemed stress‑induced hyperglycaemia rather than primary DKA. | "stress‑induced hyperglycemia r/o ketosis‑prone type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM)"  
3. Orbital cellulitis was diagnosed on day 2 when right‑eye swelling appeared; vancomycin was added, but lack of rapid improvement and necrotic tissue later argued against a purely bacterial process. | "right orbital cellulitis, vancomycin (renal dose adjusted) was added"  
4. Acute kidney injury was attributed to pre‑renal azotemia from dehydration secondary to hyperglycaemia, rather than intrinsic renal disease. | "pre‑renal AKI"  
5. Later bacterial sepsis (MRSA) was identified from wound cultures after debridement, but this occurred after the diagnostic window and did not explain the early orbital findings. | "culture from wound site in the face would eventually grow Methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA)"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies amelanotic metastatic melanoma, which is NOT among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE. The patient also had COVID-19 (a SELECTED disease), but that infection was already confirmed early and is not the mystery to be solved in this teaching case. Hence the final diagnosis will be formatted as “metastatic melanoma -> OUT_OF_SCOPE”.
2. Best Breakpoint: Include all information up to the point just before the pathology result is disclosed. Stop after describing the patient's awareness of rapid mass growth, physical‑exam characteristics, and that the soft‑tissue nodule was surgically excised and sent for pathology. Do NOT reveal the statement “The pathological diagnosis was amelanotic metastatic melanoma…”.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors highlighted that the chest‑wall nodule was initially “of indeterminate significance and etiology”, noted its rapid enlargement, and later demonstrated melanoma by morphologic and immunophenotypic features (S100, Melan‑A/Mart‑1, HMB45). Competing possibilities such as a benign soft‑tissue tumor or postoperative hematoma were considered, with the latter invoked to explain postoperative enlargement on PET.
case_prompt:
A 50‑year‑old physician and frontline COVID‑19 hospitalist presented on 17 July 2020 with flu‑like symptoms and tested positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by nasopharyngeal RT‑PCR. He required hospitalization for hypoxemia and received remdesivir, convalescent plasma, and later invasive mechanical ventilation for ARDS. His past medical history was notable for chronic dapsone therapy for dermatitis. On examination the child was drowsy, irritable, with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 12/15, facial asymmetry, and non‑purulent conjunctivitis. Vital signs were within normal limits. Lumbar puncture yielded blood‑stained cerebrospinal fluid with no white blood cells, numerous red blood cells, protein 52.87 mg/dL (reference 15–45), glucose 4.22 mmol/L (approximately 2/3 of serum), sterile culture, and no pathogen DNA/RNA detected by PCR. Multiple opportunistic infections led to suspicion of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, so further research was undergone. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors used microscopic morphology (oval yeast without hyphae), temperature‑dependent growth patterns on CHROMagar, and colony morphology to differentiate C. victoriae from C. glabrata and other Candida spp.; definitive species identification was achieved by ITS sequencing and BLAST comparison.
case_prompt: A 58‑year‑old menopausal woman and farmer with a 10‑year history of depression and uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with a 5‑day history of vulvar itching and vaginal discharge. On admission she reported thin white discharge, an odor, and intense vulvar itching. Physical examination of the vulvar structures revealed thin white exudate with odor and itching. Two vaginal swab specimens were collected with sterile cotton‑tipped swabs and transported to the parasitology laboratory within 2 hours for yeast isolation. Direct microscopic examination with 10 % KOH demonstrated oval yeast cells. The specimens were cultured on CHROMagar Candida and incubated at 20‑25 °C and 35 °C. After 2 days at 20‑25 °C, mauve colonies that were smooth, glossy, and 0.5‑1 mm in diameter appeared, appearing indistinguishable from Candida glabrata colonies. Microscopy of the cultured colonies after 48 hours showed oval yeast (3‑5 µm × 2‑3 µm), occurring singly or in clusters, without true hyphae or pseudohyphae. No growth was observed on CHROMagar Candida at 35 °C. Subculture on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 20‑25 °C for 48 hours yielded cream‑colored, slightly mucoid, highly glossy colonies; after 3 days the colonies turned pale yellow‑pink. Complete blood count and liver function tests were normal. Serologies for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative. Fasting blood glucose was 9.13 mmol/L.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Candida vulvovaginitis common in diabetic women, suggested by whitish discharge, itching, and KOH showing oval yeast | "examination results with 10% KOH revealed the presence of oval yeast."
2. Candida glabrata considered because colony morphology on CHROMagar at 20‑25 °C resembled it | "mauve colonies emerged, displaying smooth, glossy, slim characteristics… making them indistinguished from Candida glabrata colonies."
3. Exclusion of Candida glabrata based on lack of growth at 35 °C, a temperature at which C. glabrata typically grows | "No growth was observed on CHROMagar Candida at 35 C."
4. Other Candida species excluded by combination of colony color change on Sabouraud agar and absence of hyphae/pseudohyphae on microscopy | "oval yeast… either single or in clusters without true hyphae or pseudohyphae."
5. Non‑yeast causes (bacterial vaginosis, Trichomonas) deemed unlikely because KOH microscopy directly demonstrated yeast rather than clue cells or motile trophozoites | "examination results with 10% KOH revealed the presence of oval yeast."

case_prompt:
A 24‑year‑old Aboriginal Australian woman presented after a tonic‑clonic seizure. Clinical features of intracranial hypertension were identified, and a microbiological diagnosis of C. gattii meningitis was made by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture and elevated serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen titres. She had no significant medical history, exercised without limitation, smoked 10 cigarettes per day (5 pack‑years), used up to five cannabis bongs daily, and worked as a manual labourer with occupational exposure to Australian flora. Chest CT showed an asymptomatic left lower lobe consolidation.

She was treated with corticosteroids, liposomal amphotericin‑B, and 5‑flucytosine, complicated by immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome and drug‑induced kidney injury, and discharged on fluconazole, prednisolone, and pneumocystis prophylaxis.

Two weeks later she returned with fever, cough, and hypoxaemia requiring low‑flow oxygen. Repeat CT demonstrated progressive upper‑lobe consolidation and widespread ground‑glass change. Bronchoscopy yielded turbid fluid with a high CMV titre (21,217 copies/mL). Microscopy, culture, and sensitivity grew Aspergillus nidulans and Staphylococcus epidermidis, both deemed contaminants. She received intravenous ganciclovir and broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and was discharged on oral fluconazole, valganciclovir, and tapering prednisolone.

Four weeks later she re‑presented with severe hypoxic respiratory failure. Comprehensive infection screening (respiratory viral panel, sputum and blood cultures) and immunodeficiency testing (lymphocyte subsets, immunoglobulins, HIV and HTLV serology) were negative. She continued smoking cannabis and cigarettes, and had no further occupational exposure. Repeat chest CT showed progressive ground‑glass opacities with inter‑lobular septal thickening producing a classic crazy‑paving pattern. Repeat bronchoscopy returned cedar‑coloured fluid; cultures and CMV titres were now unremarkable. Despite broad‑spectrum antimicrobials and corticosteroids, her oxygen requirement rose to FiO₂ 80 % via high‑flow nasal cannula. The rare association between cryptococcosis and PAP due to GM‑CSF antibodies was considered. A subsequent bronchoalveolar lavage harvested PAS‑positive sediment using a PAS with diastase protocol. Testing for anti‑GM‑CSF antibodies was performed by a neutralisation assay using patient serum and recombinant human GM‑CSF.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. CMV pulmonary infection was considered because of a high CMV titre in bronchoalveolar lavage. | "Bronchoscopy yielded turbid fluid with high CMV titre (21,217 copies/mL)."
2. Aspergillus nidulans and Staphylococcus epidermidis were isolated but deemed contaminants, making primary fungal or bacterial pneumonia unlikely. | "Microscopy, culture and sensitivity yielded growth of Aspergillus nidulans and Staphylococcus epidermidis . Both organisms were deemed contaminants."
3. Broad infectious etiologies were excluded after negative respiratory viral panel, sputum, and blood cultures on the third admission. | "Investigation for infection (respiratory viral panel, sputum culture and blood culture) ... were negative."
4. Underlying immunodeficiency was ruled out by normal lymphocyte subsets, immunoglobulin levels, and negative HIV‑ and HTLV‑serology. | "Immunodeficiency (lymphocyte subsets, immunoglobulin levels, HIV‑serology and HTLV‑serology) were negative."
5. Cryptococcal meningitis, while present, did not explain the progressive diffuse ground‑glass infiltrates and crazy‑paving pattern. | "Microbiological diagnosis of C. gattii meningitis was made ... but the patient later developed worsening respiratory failure with characteristic CT findings."
6. Autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis was favored due to the classic crazy‑paving CT pattern, cedar‑coloured lavage fluid, PAS‑positive sediment, and confirmed anti‑GM‑CSF antibodies. | "CT chest demonstrated progressive ground glass opacities with inter‑lobular septal thickening, the classical crazy‑paving pattern ... bronchoscopy with lavage of cedar‑brown fluid contained PAS‑positive sediment ... Testing for anti‑GM‑CSF antibodies ... confirming the diagnosis of autoimmune‑PAP."

2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation after the high‑resolution chest CT report and the decision to start empiric TMP‑SMX and steroids, i.e., before any BAL microbiology results are disclosed. This gives the learner sufficient clinical, radiologic, and laboratory clues (advanced HIV with CD4 = 1 cells/µL, bilateral ground‑glass opacities, negative bacterial antigens) to deduce PCP without revealing the definitive BAL findings.

case_prompt: A 56‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with gradual onset dyspnea, cough, and fever. His past medical history was notable for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from a 20‑pack‑year smoking history and HIV infection diagnosed three years earlier during treatment for pulmonary actinomycosis; he had not received any follow‑up or antiretroviral therapy. On admission his blood pressure was 110/56 mm Hg, heart rate 110 beats/min, and SpO₂ 82 % on room air. He was alert (Glasgow coma scale 15) with no focal neurologic deficits. Oral examination revealed white lesions on the tongue, palate, and oropharynx consistent with candidiasis; papular lesions in a healing phase were noted on his back. Lung auscultation disclosed scattered crackles. Arterial blood gas on 2 L O₂ showed pH 7.45, PaO₂ 73 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 39 mm Hg, HCO₃⁻ 27 mEq/L, lactate 1.1 mmol/L, and an A‑a O₂ gradient of 77.9 mm Hg. Laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytes 4.5 × 10³/µL (lymphocytes 0.6 × 10³/µL), LDH 330 U/L, CRP 7.9 mg/dL, CD4⁺ count 1 cell/µL, CD4/CD8 ratio 0, and HIV viral load >92 000 copies. Serologies for syphilis, Toxoplasma gondii, Leishmania, hepatitis B and C were negative; urine antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella were also negative. High‑resolution chest CT revealed bilateral ground‑glass opacities. Given the advanced HIV status and the imaging appearance suggestive of Pneumocystis pneumonia, empiric trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole and systemic corticosteroids were initiated.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (target) – the combination of profound CD4⁺ lymphopenia, bilateral ground‑glass opacities on CT, and the clinical picture of sub‑acute dyspnea in an untreated HIV patient prompted empiric therapy. | "Since the patient was a person living with HIV without any follow‑up or treatment and the imaging studies were suggestive of PCP, empirical trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole ... were started."
2. Bacterial community‑acquired pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Legionella) – considered because of fever and cough, but excluded by negative urine antigen tests and lack of lobar consolidation. | "Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella urine antigen tests were also negative."
3. Other opportunistic fungal infection (Cryptococcus neoformans) – possible given oral candidiasis and severe immunosuppression, but not identified until BAL culture; later shown to coexist. | "BAL fluid analysis was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii (by PCR), Cryptococcus neoformans (by culture), and multidrug‑resistant Escherichia coli (by culture)."
4. Bacterial sepsis with multidrug‑resistant Escherichia coli – cultured from BAL, indicating a secondary bacterial infection, but the dominant pulmonary pattern was consistent with PCP. | "BAL fluid analysis was positive for ... multidrug‑resistant Escherichia coli (by culture)."

case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old male smoker with diffuse atheromatosis presented with gradually worsening intracranial hypertension. Biopsy of a left occipital lesion revealed a WHO grade III‑IV glioma near the left ventricular atrium, deemed inoperable. He received 60 Gy brain radiotherapy with corticosteroids, tolerated well, and temozolomide was planned.

Weeks later he developed left hip and buttock pain. MRI suggested corticosteroid‑induced aseptic osteonecrosis of the left femoral head, accompanied by lower‑limb edema. Ultrasound showed a left hip joint effusion and excluded deep‑vein thrombosis. Fever ensued, but all bacterial cultures were negative. Neurologically he showed apathy, drowsiness, memory problems attributed to radiotherapy and opioid analgesics. He was transferred to the infectious disease unit, where a new left hemiparesis was noted. Brain CT showed multifocal hypodensities compatible with cerebral abscesses; lumbar puncture revealed normal cell count and negative bacterial studies. Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics and intravenous acyclovir were started, but his consciousness deteriorated. Cerebral MRI confirmed multiple lesions suggestive of abscesses.

He was admitted to the ICU for septic shock. MRI of the left lower limb demonstrated necrotizing fasciitis with myonecrosis; thoracic CT revealed multiple lung lesions consistent with septic emboli. Surgical care was undertaken for extensive left‑leg cellulitis. Poly‑bacterial intestinal flora was cultured from the necrotizing tissue, suggesting an anoperineal portal of entry. Empiric poly‑antibiotic therapy was continued, along with intravenous voriconazole for presumed fungal brain involvement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial sepsis with septic emboli considered due to lung lesions and necrotizing fasciitis, but cultures from CSF and blood remained negative, and the lung lesions were not definitively bacterial. | "The bacteriological examination was negative."  
2. Cryptococcosis and toxoplasmosis evaluated as possible CNS fungal causes; both were ruled out by negative mycological and parasitological examinations of CSF. | "Mycological and parasitological examinations were negative for cryptococcosis and toxoplasmosis..."  
3. Drug‑induced neurotoxicity from radiotherapy and morphine considered for the initial neurological decline, but imaging demonstrated new multifocal lesions, pointing toward an infectious process. | "A neurological syndrome appeared, consisting of apathy, drowsiness, mnesic troubles, likely secondary to the cerebral radiotherapy and morphinic painkillers."  
4. Primary fungal CNS infection other than Aspergillus (e.g., Candida) was less likely given the pattern of multiple cerebral abscesses and the absence of typical candida dissemination. | "A probabilistic biantibiotic therapy was established, in association with an intravenous antiherpetic treatment." (implying lack of specific antifungal coverage at that stage)  
5. Invasive aspergillosis ultimately supported by repeated positive galactomannan antigenemia and tissue demonstrating Grocott‑positive, branched hyphae, confirming Aspergillus as the etiologic agent. | "During the infectious investigation, an aspergillar antigenaemia returned positive, confirmed on two other samples, suggestive of invasive aspergillosis."; "PAS and Grocott‑positive mycelial strands were brought to light, often surrounded with polynuclear cells. ... the branched‑out aspect of filaments ... suggested mycosis due to Aspergillus fumigates."

case_prompt:
A 31‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department with progressive dyspnea and a productive cough of 4 months’ duration, accompanied by decreased appetite and 50‑lb weight loss over 5 months. He had no significant past medical or surgical history and was not on any medications. He quit smoking two months ago; he denied excessive alcohol use, recreational drugs, and multiple sexual partners. He worked as a janitor in an automobile parts factory. He had previously served in the army and was stationed in Hawaii, where he had visited a prostitute on several occasions.

On arrival his temperature was 99.9 °F, blood pressure 128/83 mm Hg, pulse 134 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 92 % on room air. He was in moderate respiratory distress but alert and cooperative. Examination showed oral thrush on the tongue and palate, no lymphadenopathy, regular heart sounds, and equal chest rise. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally with rales and dullness to percussion in the lower lung fields. Neurologic examination was otherwise normal.

Laboratory studies revealed: WBC 13,900/µL, hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, platelets 370 × 10³/µL, sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, CO₂ 17 mmol/L, BUN 155 mg/dL, creatinine 8.9 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas on 3 L nasal cannula showed pH 7.39, pCO₂ 32.2 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 19.1 mmol/L, pO₂ 74.5 mmHg. Chest radiograph demonstrated diffuse bilateral reticulonodular opacities. HIV testing was positive with a CD4 count < 5 cells/µL and viral load 1,180,000 copies/mL.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Opportunistic pneumonia due to Pneumocystis jirovecii is most likely given advanced AIDS (CD4 < 200), subacute dyspnea, weight loss, diffuse reticulonodular infiltrates, and lack of focal consolidation. | "Grocott's methenamine silver stain of the washings demonstrated Pneumocystis jiroveci"
2. Cytomegalovirus pneumonia was considered but excluded because PCR for cytomegalovirus was negative. | "Polymerase chain reactions for … cytomegalovirus … were negative."
3. Epstein‑Barr virus, Herpes simplex virus, and JC virus infections were considered in the differential for opportunistic pulmonary disease but ruled out by negative PCR. | "Polymerase chain reactions for Epstein‑Barr virus, Herpes simplex virus, … John Cunningham (JC) virus were negative."
4. Syphilis, toxoplasmosis, and cryptococcal infection were evaluated as possible opportunistic etiologies but serologies/antigen tests were negative. | "Nontreponemal serological screening for syphilis (VDRL), toxoplasmosis antibody, and Cryptococcus antigen titers were negative."
5. Neoplastic processes (e.g., primary CNS lymphoma) were excluded by normal neuroimaging. | "CT of the head did not show any intracranial mass, hemorrhage, or other acute findings."

case_prompt: A 40‑year‑old female presented with fever, loss of appetite, burning epigastrium, and a non‑productive cough of seven days’ duration. Examination revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly. She was provisionally diagnosed with acid peptic disease. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7 g/dL, ESR 58 mm/hr, total leukocyte count 3,600/µL with microcytic, hypochromic red cells, normal white cells, and reduced platelets. Peripheral smear demonstrated a few late normoblasts, 6 % myelocytes and metamyelocytes, but no hemoparasites or immature blasts. Bone‑marrow aspiration was performed. Marrow was hypercellular with erythroid hyperplasia; myelopoiesis and megakaryocytes were normal. Granulomas containing epithelioid cells were identified, and encapsulated round organisms suggestive of Cryptococcus were seen around the granulomas. Acid‑fast bacilli were not demonstrable. Special stains (mucicarmine, PAS) highlighted the yeast forms. The report concluded a chronic granulomatous infection with cryptococcosis and recommended HIV testing.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial suspicion of acid‑peptic disease based on epigastric burning and cough | "She was provisionally diagnosed as a case of acid peptic disease."
2. Anemia and pancytopenia suggested a marrow process, prompting aspiration | "Hemoglobin of 7 gm/dl... total leucocyte count of 3600/cu.mm... Platelets were reduced."
3. Granulomatous inflammation raised concern for tuberculosis, but acid‑fast bacilli were absent | "Acid fast bacilli were not demonstrable."
4. Identification of encapsulated yeast organisms pointed toward cryptococcosis, an opportunistic infection seen in immunocompromised hosts | "Encapsulated round organisms suggestive of Cryptococcus were also seen around the granulomas."
5. Presence of cryptococcosis and unexplained cytopenias prompted evaluation for underlying immunodeficiency, leading to HIV testing | "It was reported as a case of chronic granulomatous infection with cryptococcosis and test for HIV was advised."
6. Positive ELISA confirmed HIV infection, establishing the underlying cause of the opportunistic fungal disease | "The ELISA test for detection of HIV was positive."

case_prompt:
A 44‑year‑old Caucasian woman with branchio‑oto‑renal (BOR) syndrome and a deceased‑donor renal transplant 20 years earlier presented to the outpatient clinic with an 11‑month history of progressive bilateral vision loss, more pronounced in the right eye and at night, accompanied by central scotoma. Updating her lens prescription did not improve symptoms. She denied ocular pain or epiphora. Visual acuity was 20/50 (right) and 20/80 (left). Slit‑lamp examination showed corneal scars from prior refractive surgery and diffuse mild corneal opacities bilaterally. Fundoscopy revealed diffuse rarefaction of the retinal pigment epithelium, consistent with high myopia, and no signs of intra‑ocular inflammation or infection. Vision later declined to 20/400 (right) and 20/200 (left). Electroretinography demonstrated ischemic changes, especially of the inner retina.

Her immunosuppression regimen included tacrolimus, azathioprine, and prednisone. She reported prior unprotected sex. Serum testing showed a VDRL titer of 1:2048 and a positive FTA‑ABS. She was admitted for further evaluation. A 52‑year‑old man with rheumatoid arthritis presented to the emergency department after one week of fevers, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, a nonproductive cough, fatigue, and one month of night sweats. He denied known tuberculosis exposure.

On admission he was afebrile, but his oxygen saturation was 85% on room air, requiring 2–3 L/min supplemental oxygen. Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count and elevated liver enzymes (AST 74 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 170 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X‑ray demonstrated diffuse reticulonodular densities with hilar lymphadenopathy. He received empiric IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin, later broadened to ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole for community‑acquired pneumonia.

Extensive infectious testing was negative: respiratory viral PCR, Histoplasma urine antigen, Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen, Legionella urine antigen, HIV 4th‑generation assay, acute hepatitis panel, serum HSV PCR, serum CMV PCR, QuantiFERON‑TB Gold, and sputum Pneumocystis jirovecii DFA. Rheumatology held methotrexate and sulfasalazine.

CT of the chest showed diffuse micronodularity in all lobes with a perilymphatic and centrilobular distribution, scattered calcified granulomas, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly—findings described as a miliary pattern. Three sputum AFB smears were negative; MTB nucleic acid amplification was nondetectable.

Bronchoscopy revealed endobronchial nodules and plaques in the left upper lobe. Biopsies were sent for aerobic, AFB, and fungal cultures. BAL Aspergillus galactomannan and Pneumocystis DFA were negative. Serum Aspergillus galactomannan, Histoplasma antigen, and Cryptococcus antigen assays were negative; serum Aspergillus fumigatus IgG was elevated (13.03 U/mL). Pathology showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation; AFB and GMS stains were negative.

Five days after bronchoscopy, Coccidioides complement‑fixation titer was 1:8, Coccidioides IgM ELISA was positive, and Coccidioides IgG ELISA was negative. An immunodiffusion assay demonstrated a partial identity reaction suggestive of cross‑reactivity. Based on these results, the patient was started on liposomal amphotericin B, while posaconazole and anidulafungin were discontinued. After one week of amphotericin B, he was transitioned to oral fluconazole 400 mg daily. His hypoxia resolved and he was discharged home.

Physical examination revealed oral thrush‑like white patches and a macular rash on the back. Renal function had acutely worsened (creatinine rose from baseline 3.0 mg/dL to >4.0 mg/dL); liver enzymes were within normal limits. Her maintenance immunosuppression consisted of prednisone 5 mg/day and azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day.

On admission, blood cultures for fungi and mycobacteria were obtained. PCR testing for CMV and EBV, a latex agglutination test for cryptococcus, and serologies for Histoplasma capsulatum and Trypanosoma cruzi were ordered. CMV antigenemia was negative, but PCR detected 546 copies of CMV DNA. A skin lesion biopsy and cultures for fungi and mycobacteria were performed. Thoraco‑abdominal CT and transthoracic echocardiogram were unremarkable. Bone‑marrow examination showed erythroid hyperplasia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy identified ulcerative esophagitis with intranuclear inclusions and focal esophageal candidiasis; fluconazole was added to the regimen.

Empiric liposomal amphotericin B was begun to cover possible histoplasmosis, and a four‑drug anti‑tuberculous regimen was added. Despite maximal support, she required mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, and subsequently developed acute hepatitis attributed to amphotericin B.
